📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s not technically winter yet, but depending on where you live, it may feel like it. For many of us, this is a time of hibernation, but for others, it’s prime time for a glow-up.

Recent findings suggest that “Winter arc” is a popular social media challenge through which people aim to improve themselves before the latest year. It typically runs from October through December, but can be started any time during the cold months. The aim is to jump-start the “new year, new me” season before the ball even drops.

Whether they call it a winter arc or not, plenty of Americans are working on self-improvement as the chill sets in. According to a fresh NerdWallet survey, conducted online by The Harris Poll, 75% of Americans say they’re working on their physical health, and 69% say the same about their finances.

Recent findings suggest that popular as it is, winter arc isn’t the only cold-weather challenge out there. The survey found that half of Americans (50%) say they’ve tried some sort of winter improvement challenge. And no one likes a challenge like Gen Z: Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) have tried a winter challenge, compared with 64% of millennials, 42% of Gen Xers and 29% of baby boomers.

Note: The survey defines Gen Zers as those 18-29; millennials, ages 30-45; Gen Xers, ages 46-61 and baby boomers, ages 62-80.

According to recent reports, but there’s a difference between starting a challenge and successfully completing one. Gen Zers reign supreme as those most likely to hop on a winter challenge. But they’re also the most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing, buy products they saw on social media in an effort to stick with the challenges and set the same financial goal more than once.

Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they:.

Recent findings suggest that have tried a winter financial challenge other than no-spend January (21%, vs. 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers).

Generally quit challenges before they finish them (59%, vs. 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers).

Recent findings suggest that expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season (90%, vs. 83% of millennials, 61% of Gen Xers and 48% of baby boomers).

Put off dealing with money until after the holidays (60%, vs. 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers).

Aren’t presently working on improving their finances, but want to make it a priority (15%, vs. 8% of millennials and 6% each of Gen Xers and baby boomers).

“Embracing the winter arc trend can be a great way to find motivation to make progress on a goal over the slower winter months,” indicates Kimberly Palmer, personal finance expert at NerdWallet. “Pick a winter challenge that aligns with a longer-term goal for the coming year.”.

Winter challenges popular with Gen Z include diet- or fitness-related challenges (29%) and self-improvement challenges, like winter arc or 75 Hard, a mental toughness challenge that runs for 75 days and includes two workouts every day, a strict diet and daily nonfiction reading (25%).

While winter arcs typically focus on physical, mental and intellectual self-improvement, Gen Z is game to try a financial challenge as well: One long-standing financial challenge — no-spend January — is more popular among younger Americans (22% of Gen Zers and 20% of millennials) than their older counterparts (12% of Gen Xers and 6% of baby boomers). As for other types of financial challenges, Gen Z is more likely than any other generation to have tried at least one: 21% compared with 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen X and 2% of baby boomers.

Of course, it’s one thing to try a challenge, during wintertime or otherwise. It’s another thing entirely to follow through and complete it. That’s the hard part for many Gen Zers.

When taking on a self-improvement challenge, the beginning tends to be easiest. You’re motivated and excited to reach goals and better yourself. But as time goes on, it’s easy to slip back into old habits or for the shine of a brand-newly introduced challenge to dim. And Gen Zers report that they are most likely to quit early.

Recent findings suggest that according to the survey, nearly 3 in 5 Gen Zers (59%) say they generally quit challenges before they finish them. That compares with 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers.

In a recent development, along with challenges in general, money goals can be difficult to follow through with, especially for younger Americans. Around two-thirds of Gen Zers (64%) say it’s been hard to stick to financial goals they’ve set in the past, compared with 52% of Gen Xers and 34% of baby boomers. Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they’ve set the same financial goal more than once because they didn’t stick with it — 33%, compared with 20% of millennials, 15% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers.

Sources indicate that this isn’t for lack of desire, though. Seven in 10 Gen Zers (70%) say they’re working on improving their finances. All generations show high levels of effort here: 76% each of millennials and Gen Xers say the same, along with 59% of baby boomers.

In a recent development, so why is it so hard to stick with money goals? One possibility is that it’s difficult to see meaningful progress on finances, particularly when you’re young. According to the survey, 65% of Gen Zers say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than on physical goals.

Recent findings suggest that this makes perfect sense for this age group — for those light on money but rich in youthfulness, desired physical changes may show up faster than financial progress. On top of that, the current job market is tough for younger Americans. Recent college grads now have a higher unemployment rate than workers in general. Even if you’re still on the job hunt, your 20s are a great time to start taking steps, however small, toward building future wealth.» MORE: I’m 25. Here’s How I Got Started Investing.

Industry observers note that “To increase your chances of success, try coordinating winter arc plans with a friend or giving yourself smaller goals along the way,” Palmer claims. “Leaning on the support or coaching from a loved one can make it easier to keep going, as can celebrating incremental progress.”.

Self-improvement is a noble pursuit. But as with most things in life, it’s easy to lose sight of the ultimate goal in favor of buying things to help you reach it.

“It’s easy to feel like a quick purchase can help us meet our goals, and sometimes a product can be a useful tool, but the reality is that true winter arc progress comes from putting in the hard work. There’s no option for ‘purchasing’ it instead,” Palmer says.

According to the survey, more than a quarter of Gen Zers (26%) say they’ve bought a product they saw on social media to help with a personal goal or challenge. This is more than any other generation: 17% of millennials, 11% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers say they’ve made social media buys for self-betterment.

It has been revealed that some self-improvement purchases may be billed on a monthly basis. More than 1 in 5 Gen Zers (23%) say they're still paying for a subscription or membership they signed up for during a past goal or challenge. This is also true for 17% of millennials, 9% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers.

Industry observers note that these challenge purchases may pile onto already higher winter expenses. A majority of Gen Zers (90%) say they expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season, more than any other generation. Top expenses include food delivery (38%), entertainment at home (35%) and indoor family entertainment (30%). A quarter of Gen Zers (25%) expect to spend more on fitness or wellness apps this winter compared to other seasons.

Sources indicate that some may be spending more to make themselves feel better during the cold, gray months. Nearly 1 in 5 Gen Zers (18%) say they tend to combat winter blues by spending money, compared with 10% of Gen Xers and 3% of baby boomers.

The holiday season is an expensive time of year for many of us, and it’s easy to sweep finances under the rug until the latest year. According to the survey, 3 in 5 Gen Zers (60%) say they generally put off dealing with money until after the holidays. This is more than any other generation: 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers say the same.

It has been revealed that even for those taking on financial challenges before the latest year hits, it’s easy for the resulting “savings” to disappear. Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually just gets spent somewhere else instead of staying “saved.” This is also true for 68% of millennials, 63% of Gen Xers and 45% of baby boomers.

Recent findings suggest that for some, the holidays are just one thing competing for their money. Over half of Gen Zers (52%) say they’d rather spend money on how they look now than save it for their future financial security. This compares with 26% of Gen Xers and 13% of baby boomers.

We don’t begrudge anyone for their desire to look and feel their best this upcoming season. But that doesn’t have to mean you can’t level up your money at the same time.

More than 2 in 5 Gen Zers (43%) say they’re putting consistent work into improving their finances, and 27% are putting some work into this, but not consistently. Moreover, 15% of Gen Zers aren’t working on improving their finances but want to make them a priority. No matter your age, here are some ideas for a financial glow-up before the spring thaw.

Sources indicate that start small if you tend to quit. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they generally quit challenges before finishing them. Early-challenge motivation can make it easy to overcommit. If you often take on challenges impulsively then peter out a few weeks later, try starting small. For example, maybe no-spend January is a stretch, but you can still save by intentionally creating two no-spend days a week.

In a recent development, move money the day you save it. Over 3 in 5 Americans (61%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually gets spent somewhere else. If you’re cutting back, transfer the difference to savings that same day, so it can’t leak out elsewhere.

Sources indicate that make money progress measurable. Half of Americans (50%) say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than physical goals. There’s a saying that what gets measured, gets managed. Choose one number to track. This might be down payment savings, debt payoff progress or an investment milestone. It may not move much month to month, but you’d be surprised at the difference a year can make, even without a ton of money each month to dedicate toward your goal.

Begin before January. More than a third of Americans (37%) say they put off dealing with money until after the holidays. Facing your finances during the often busy and expensive final months of the year can be daunting, but don’t put your head in the sand until after the holiday credit card balances come due. Put a cap on your winter spending before the latest year to avoid going overboard during the tempting sales this time of year.

“If you’re trying to choose a winter arc, pick one that’s realistic but also a stretch goal, so it’s satisfying to accomplish while not being completely out of reach,” Palmer suggests. “Chances are you’ll be glad with what you got done over the colder months when springtime hits.”.

Latest Update: AI Food Images Have A Business Upside. They Also Have A Trust Problem

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Claeys is CEO of QR TIGER, MENU TIGER and GiftLips.
  • A few weeks ago, I walked into a canteen and ordered tacos.
  • According to recent reports, it wasn’t a terrible meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Claeys is CEO of QR TIGER, MENU TIGER and GiftLips. He also hosts Stay QRious, a podcast about QR code best practices.

A few weeks ago, I walked into a canteen and ordered tacos. The photo demonstrated a full plate loaded with fresh toppings. What arrived was different: smaller portions, fewer toppings and a flat presentation.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t a terrible meal. But the photograph had promised something else.

It has been revealed that that mismatch is becoming more common as restaurants turn to AI-generated food images. Operators can now generate food photos quickly, sometimes without the high cost or lead time of professional food photography.

Recent findings suggest that the economic pressure is real. U.S. restaurant sales are projected to reach $1.55 trillion in 2026, even as operators continue to face uneven traffic and rising food and labor costs.

Recent findings suggest that when every dollar counts, faster and cheaper visual content is understandably attractive. But a menu image isn’t just decoration. It’s a direct promise to the customer about what they’ll receive. When that promise is broken, the short-term savings come at the cost of customer trust.

There’s another problem with synthetic food imagery: It doesn’t make the meal more appealing.

In a recent development, A 2025 study in Appetite examined how people responded to AI-generated food images and found evidence of an “uncanny valley effect.” Images feel unsettling when they look highly realistic but don’t accurately reflect the food in reality. When an AI burger looks too smooth or sauce looks like plastic, the human brain notices. Instead of making people hungry, it makes the food feel less appealing.

A CNN reporter noted a similar reaction from an ad sales worker who, while browsing a Hollywood market, described AI vendor images as having a “too-perfect, almost rubbery aesthetic” that made her doubt the quality of the actual food.

According to recent reports, traditional food photography has always involved impeccable lighting and styling to make real food look good. The difference with generative AI is that it invents items from scratch.

In a recent development, generative AI tools learn from large amounts of text and visual data to create realistic-looking images, but doesn’t maintain the physical consistency of the food they depict. An AI generator can easily add bigger portions, extra toppings or textures.

Sources indicate that this creates legal risk. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) evaluates advertising based on the overall impression an image gives to customers. If a digital menu photo creates an expectation that the kitchen can’t meet, it contributes to a misleading advertising claim.

After years of studying the restaurant industry, I’ve seen how quick they adapt: They add new dishes, update seasonal menus and move their menus online, often without the time or resources to create everything from scratch.

Recent findings suggest that AI can help remove some of that friction. AI-assisted menu digitization helps restaurants convert existing printed menus into digital versions faster. AI interprets the restaurant’s existing dishes, prices, descriptions and structure, then provides images while owners review and edit the results. It speeds up conversion without inventing menu content.

Cost is another factor. For independent restaurants and startups, professional food photography can be expensive. A small food photography shoot is estimated at around $350 to $500, while AI-generated images provide a lower-cost temporary option. Restaurants can also use AI to test different plating, backgrounds or visual concepts before investing in a photoshoot.

The key is knowing where AI fits. Once real photos are available, replace the AI images and match the final visuals with what customers will actually receive.

Industry observers note that food images can influence dining decisions. In fact, research from the International Journal of Hospitality Management found that food photos give diners a clearer idea of what to expect than descriptions alone.​.

It has been revealed that for recently added dishes or menu items that need a visual, AI-generated images can be a placeholder while restaurants build their visual library.​ But it needs careful consideration. A Chicago deli faced backlash for using temporary AI-generated sandwich images that indicated misleading food details. Detailed prompts may help produce more accurate images, but restaurants should still make sure the images reflect the actual food they serve.

Start with a photo of the actual dish. AI can improve the lighting, background or setting. Keep the ingredients, portion size, toppings and overall appearance accurate. The idea is similar to traditional food photo editing, where adjustments improve the presentation without changing the actual dish.

Recent findings suggest that as AI images become harder to distinguish, give customers the context of what they’re seeing. Social platforms such as Facebook, LinkedIn and Instagram have done the same. A note such as “AI-generated image for illustrative purposes. Actual dishes may vary.” can provide context. But disclosure doesn’t make an inaccurate image acceptable.

According to recent reports, images should support the menu, not provide facts about the food. Ingredients and allergen information should always come from the restaurant and be checked separately. AI images can change or add visual details, so restaurants must have written information for accurate allergen details.

Menu images can help customers ideate what their food will look like. Whether the image is AI-generated or not, it should look appealing without creating expectations the restaurant can’t meet.

According to recent reports, when accuracy matters more than visual polish, AI may be better used behind the scenes. Restaurants can use AI for menu management, analysis, forecasting and other operational tasks where the technology supports the business without shaping customer expectations.

The standard is simple: The food shown on the menu should reflect the food customers expect to receive. AI makes restaurant imagery faster and more affordable, but those savings don’t justify misleading customers.

AI should remove friction for restaurants without removing their control, and appealing doesn’t have to mean fictional.​.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

According to recent reports, the results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. With Democrats to Control Congress, Is It Better to Buy Bitcoin or an Index Fund?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that control of Congress just changed poltical hands in a big way, and, much as with all major changes, it's no surprise that it's making some investors a bit uneasy.
  • So, in light of the congressional switchover and the many uncertainties in the market right now, does it make more sense to buy Bitcoin, or an index fund?
  • Industry observers note that first, let's establish some basic facts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Alex Carchidi – Nov 18, 2026 at 7:45AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Bitcoin ›.

Sources indicate that control of Congress just changed poltical hands in a big way, and, much as with all major changes, it's no surprise that it's making some investors a bit uneasy. Many holders of Bitcoin (BTC -3.10%) openly worry that the newly introduced Democratic majority will have a grudge against crypto due to the Trump administration's embrace of it. At the same time, index fund owners, even for the funds tracking the entire market like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.27%), are concerned about high valuations, persistent inflation, and artificial intelligence (AI), and those worries are amplified by widespread (and overstated) impressions that Democratic congresses tend to be bad for asset prices.

So, in light of the congressional switchover and the many uncertainties in the market right now, does it make more sense to buy Bitcoin, or an index fund?

Industry observers note that first, let's establish some basic facts. A party gaining control of both houses of Congress is not something that's strongly associated with the market tanking or flying afterward.

From 1955 to 2023, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -1.03%) delivered a total return of 8.6% annually in years when a Republican president was balanced by a Democratic Congress (and one of those years, during the 2008 financial crisis, skews those results to the downside significantly). Patience and consistency were still the most important traits that investors needed to have to build their portfolios during those periods.

Sources indicate that for Bitcoin, the last time Democrats held control of both congressional chambers, through all of 2021 and 2022, it fell 48%. But don't read too much into that; during the same time, the crypto industry was being rocked by the spectacular collapse of the FTX exchange, and Bitcoin was in one of its bear markets after a strong upward trend in the prior years.

According to recent reports, still, Senator Elizabeth Warren, a loud critic of the cryptocurrency industry, is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee when the newly introduced Congress is seated in 2027. She's also one of the senators that detractors traditionally single out as being noxious to stock and crypto prices. A closer inspection reveals that Warren's recent crypto scrutiny has focused on allegedly corrupt practices of some crypto businesses, like those associated with the Trump family and the Trump administration. Similarly, Warren has been in politics for a long time, and the stock market has still on average increased annually during her tenure.

So, it's my assessment that many of the politics-related concerns about Bitcoin and the U.S. stock market are heavily overstated despite being modestly grounded in reality.

Politics aside, there are other reasons that investors propose for being a bit squeamish about buying either Bitcoin or an index fund.

The lofty valuation of the market is a big and real concern. One valuation metric, the Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio, divides the S&P 500's price by its average inflation-adjusted earnings during the prior decade, and it was near 40 on Nov. 17, whereas its long-run mean is 17.5. High valuations tend to predict lower future returns until either earnings catch up or share prices go down; Vanguard's forecast as of Sept. 30 is for  U.S. stocks to return 4.8% to 6.8% per year during the next decade, suggesting a lower-than-average annual return.

Bitcoin is having somewhat of the opposite problem. With its price at $63,360 as of Nov. 17, it's almost 50% below its peak set in October 2025. Its price now is just a bit higher than it was five years ago. That can make it hard to stomach making a purchase.

If you must pick between buying Bitcoin and shares of an index fund, pick the index fund.

It has been revealed that an index fund tracking the S&P 500 holds shares of roughly 500 large companies, so its value rests on corporate profits even if valuations shrink. Furthermore, a committee at index provider S&P Dow Jones Indices periodically swaps out companies that no longer meet its criteria, and companies whose market value is growing carry more weight in the index. In contrast, Bitcoin has no cash flow, so its price depends on latest buyers willing to pay the market price, and it's obviously harder to attract them when its price isn't climbing steadily.

Of course, most people needn't choose only one of these assets. Anyone buying Bitcoin should already own plenty of index fund shares, and Bitcoin is also something that should be a limited part of most diversified portfolios already.

Have $1,000? This Beaten-Down Biotech Has 4 Phase 3 Obesity Trials Underway.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than Viking Therapeutics ›.
  • Phase 3 trials are always interesting because of their proximity to approval and ultimate commercialization of drugs, and particularly so when it involves one with a huge total addressable market (TAM) such as obesity.
  • The four phase 3 trials comprise two ongoing 78-week trials of VK2735 in subcutaneous form (obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes; results due in 2027) and two recently started 68-week trials in oral form (results more likely in 2028) for the same indications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lee Samaha – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:00AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Viking Therapeutics ›.

Phase 3 trials are always interesting because of their proximity to approval and ultimate commercialization of drugs, and particularly so when it involves one with a huge total addressable market (TAM) such as obesity. In addition, the drug in question here, Viking Therapeutics' VK2735, is in a class that already includes one blockbuster drug: Eli Lilly's (LLY -0.32%) tirzepatide (Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for obesity with type 2 diabetes), which is approved. All these developments make Viking Therapeutics an attractive stock for investors. Here's why.

The four phase 3 trials comprise two ongoing 78-week trials of VK2735 in subcutaneous form (obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes; results due in 2027) and two recently started 68-week trials in oral form (results more likely in 2028) for the same indications.

NASDAQ · As of 9:31 AM ET 11/18/26.

The trials are part of management's strategy to potentially offer VK2735 across a range of dosing options, including a dual formulation option in which initial weight loss from subcutaneous dosing could be followed by maintenance dosing with a more convenient oral form.

In a recent development, investors have high hopes for the glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist, on the back of the success of Eli Lilly's GLP-1/GIP agonist, tirzepatide, and the phase 2 data from the VK2735 trials, which indicate it could achieve a steeper rate of weight loss than tirzepatide. I use cautionary language, as any comparison between two independent trials (let alone a phase 2 and a phase 3) should be accompanied by qualifications.

Sources indicate that that noted, VK2735 has demonstrated an impressive ability to produce rapid weight loss, as confirmed in a recent small 33-week maintenance study, in which an initial 21-week subcutaneous dose was followed by a subcutaneous maintenance dose over 12 weeks. An exploratory cohort in this trial reported 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks.

The success of this maintenance trial, the first part of a two-part trial, encouraged management to raise a net $547.8 million in a well-received stock offering at $35 and convertible senior notes.

As good as the maintenance trial was, investors should note the second part of the trial (ongoing) is arguably more vital, as it involves an initial 21-week subcutaneous dose followed by oral dosing over 12 weeks. The point is that phase 2 of oral VK2735 had questionable tolerability (a 20% discontinuation rate due to adverse events in the treated group), and Viking will have to demonstrate better tolerability in the maintenance trial and the phase 3 oral trials.

I previously outlined the math showing how a $10,000 investment in Viking Therapeutics could grow to $47,800 in 2030; it follows that a $1,000 investment could grow to $4,780.

That's the bullish case scenario, but investors always need to consider the risk that the phase 3 trials will fail to meet their primary endpoints or could deliver efficacy or tolerability data that negatively impacts the commercial appeal of the drug, not least because it's a highly competitive market with Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and others developing rival drugs.

The strongest case for the stock isn't that VK2735 will become a blockbuster drug, but rather that even if it captures only a relatively small share of the market, it will be enough to drive a significant increase in the share price of the $3.5 billion market-cap firm.

It has been revealed that it could do so provided its phase 3 trials deliver on the weight loss generated in the phase 2 trials and, ideally, some improved tolerability data in the maintenance study, which is due to report results next year. Investors will need to be patient, as the oral trial results (crucial to the dual formulation strategy) aren't likely to be available until 2028. The long-term potential is obvious, and Viking Therapeutics could always be acquired by a larger manufacturer seeking a late-stage obesity drug candidate.

#27371. More Subscribers Won’t Save Your Business: The Trap Of Vanity Growth

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (753 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

More Subscribers Won’t Save Your Business: The Trap Of Vanity Growth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vasudeva Akula, VOZIQ AI cofounder and head of data science.
  • For years, customer acquisition has been treated as a straightforward equation: Generate demand, identify prospects most likely to convert, optimize sales and measure success through conversion rates, customer acquisition cost and new customers added.
  • According to recent reports, compare these two leads: One is highly likely to convert but switches to a competitor before the acquisition cost is recovered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vasudeva Akula, VOZIQ AI cofounder and head of data science. Helps recurring revenue businesses improve customer retention using ML.

For years, customer acquisition has been treated as a straightforward equation: Generate demand, identify prospects most likely to convert, optimize sales and measure success through conversion rates, customer acquisition cost and new customers added. These metrics are still important, but especially for subscription businesses, they leave leaders in the dark about whether the business wins today are contributing to tomorrow’s growth.

According to recent reports, compare these two leads: One is highly likely to convert but switches to a competitor before the acquisition cost is recovered. Another has a lower conversion propensity but stays loyal for years. Businesses that optimize acquisition only for conversion can become more efficient at winning customers without becoming better at building a valuable customer base. This gap between acquisition and long-term value becomes more consequential as subscription businesses try to improve their growth trajectory against headwinds.

In this article, I’ll discuss this disconnect and provide three actionable steps that are proven to bridge the gap between acquisition and long-term value.

It has been revealed that A lead-scoring model can become increasingly accurate at predicting purchases without identifying which customers will generate lasting value. When success is measured at the point of sale, a customer who stays for years and one who leaves within months can both count as successful acquisitions. Without customer outcomes informing acquisition decisions, businesses can improve conversion performance without improving the long-term economics of their customer base.​.

It has been revealed that retention and service teams see which customers leave early, which remain for years and which generate sustained value. Acquisition teams, meanwhile, work with prospect characteristics and conversion data.

When these datasets are disconnected, customer outcomes don’t consistently influence future targeting. The same weaknesses can persist across successive acquisition cohorts, even when historical evidence could help identify prospects more likely to become valuable customers.

Recent findings suggest that closing the feedback loop means using retention outcomes to identify the characteristics associated with valuable, long-lasting customer relationships, then applying those insights to future prospect evaluation and lead scoring. As new cohorts mature, their outcomes provide further evidence to refine future acquisition decisions.

According to recent reports, increasing acquisition alone may therefore fail to deliver sustainable growth. Reducing avoidable departures and expanding existing relationships can also contribute to growth. The outcome depends on how effectively the business acquires customers, sustains relationships and increases their value together.​.

Conversion rates and customer acquisition cost remain important, but leaders should evaluate them alongside outcomes. How many acquired customers remain after 90 days or one year? How much value do they generate relative to acquisition and service costs? Which acquisition sources produce stronger long-term outcomes?

These measures help distinguish acquisition volume from acquisition quality and reveal whether better conversion translates into stronger customer economics.

Customer outcomes should inform future targeting and lead scoring. If particular customer characteristics or acquisition sources are associated with stronger long-term outcomes, that evidence should influence where the business invests its acquisition resources.

Predictive customer lifetime value (PCLV) can help estimate the economic value a customer is expected to generate over time. Used alongside conversion propensity, acquisition costs and observed outcomes, it helps businesses evaluate both the likelihood of winning a customer and the potential value of that relationship. The goal isn’t to replace conversion metrics with a single prediction but to make acquisition decisions using a more complete view of customer economics and refine them as actual outcomes become available.

It has been revealed that each of the “get,” “keep” and “grow” life cycle stages require different strategies, but their effectiveness depends on how they inform one another. “Keep” helps identify which customers stay and generate lasting value. “Get” uses those insights to find prospects with similar characteristics, while “grow” focuses on expanding the value of established relationships.

When these levers share a common view of customer value, acquisition is informed by actual customer outcomes, and growth decisions become more closely connected to long-term economics.​.

Acquiring more customers alone won’t improve the quality of growth. Long-term growth and a competitive edge will come from learning from each customer relationship and using that knowledge to acquire the right customers. And based on data center readiness, the durability of demand, and customer access to capital, Nvidia raised its outlook for growth in the coming full year to 75% from its earlier estimate of 70%.

All of this is reassuring for investors who might have worried about a potential flagging of demand.

Meanwhile, Nvidia shares look dirt cheap, trading at a little over 16x forward earnings estimates.

Sentiment, rather than earnings figures and market position, may guide the stock price. Huang also must testify before Congress following allegations of his relationship with a possible spy. Any information gathered could lead to more government scrutiny concerning Nvidia or even greater regulation.

In a recent development, the 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst stated, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

  • Industry observers note that intel focuses on designing its own processors while opening its factories to external customers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:08AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Intel ›.

Recent findings suggest that the chip industry is undergoing a massive shift as artificial intelligence and local manufacturing take center stage. Choosing between Intel (INTC +1.18%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +2.32%) requires weighing a turnaround story against a market leader.

Industry observers note that intel focuses on designing its own processors while opening its factories to external customers. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing serves as a pure-play foundry, producing high-end chips for nearly every major player among semiconductor stocks. Both companies are central to the global tech supply chain but offer very different risk and reward profiles.

Intel designs and manufactures a wide range of processors, accelerators, and software solutions for the modern computing world. Under its latest strategy, the tech giant is combining its internal chip design with a massive expansion of its foundry services to manufacture chips for other businesses. Its customer base is diverse, including distributors, original equipment manufacturers, and cloud service providers across sectors like healthcare, finance, and telecommunications.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached approximately $59.9 billion, representing revenue growth of nearly 12.1% compared to the previous period. However, the company faced significant headwinds, reporting a net loss of roughly $12 billion during this time frame. This result highlights the high costs associated with its ongoing efforts to regain a leading position in the semiconductor market.

As of Intel's December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.4, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio is approximately 2, indicating the ability to cover short-term financial obligations with assets that can be converted to cash within a year. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was approximately negative $4.9 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 25.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as a pure-play foundry, focusing exclusively on manufacturing semiconductors designed by its customers. It serves the most demanding segments of the market, including smartphones and high-performance artificial intelligence applications, from its base in Taiwan and facilities worldwide. By acting as a manufacturer for others, the manufacturer avoids competing directly with its clients while maintaining a critical role in the global tech supply chain.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $150.2 billion, an increase of approximately 36.1%. This growth translated into net income of close to $76.8 billion, resulting in a robust net margin of roughly 51.1%. These figures demonstrate the strong demand for the advanced manufacturing nodes that the firm provides to its diverse customer base.

It has been revealed that as of TSM's December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was roughly 2.5, reflecting a healthy cushion for meeting short-term liabilities. The company maintains a conservative debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.2, showing that its total debt is low relative to its equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $30.1 billion, providing substantial capital to reinvest in the next generation of chip technology.

It has been revealed that intel faces intense competition from companies like NVIDIA (NVDA -0.44%) and AMD (AMD +2.80%), as well as hyperscalers who are increasingly designing their own custom silicon. The firm is also navigating legal challenges, including shareholder lawsuits filed in November 2026 alleging concealment of manufacturing and inventory problems. High capital intensity and the operational risks of its turnaround strategy remain significant hurdles as it builds out fresh leading-edge factories while relying on sole-source suppliers like ASML (ASML +1.08%) for critical tools.

Sources indicate that taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is exposed to risks associated with the high concentration of its manufacturing facilities in a single geographic region. This concentration creates sensitivity to geopolitical tensions and potential supply chain disruptions that could impact its global operations. Additionally, the manufacturer must continually invest billions in upcoming technology nodes to stay ahead of rivals, which entails significant capital risk if demand for high-end chips from major customers like Apple (AAPL +0.92%) or NVIDIA fluctuates.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing looks cheaper on a forward P/E basis, while Intel has a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

It has been revealed that A large part of the reason Intel reported that $12 billion loss is because it's in the midst of a turnaround. It's pivoting toward providing chip manufacturing services for third parties. In order to do so, the chipmaker is having to shell out a lot of money to build fabrication plants. Intel even suspended its dividend a few years ago in pursuit of this latest strategy. That spending will likely continue, as turning around a ship of Intel's size is neither a fast nor an easy endeavor.

Now, let's see how each stock has performed over the past 10 years:.

Intel's stock is miles behind Taiwan Semiconductor's, and worse yet, it hasn't even kept pace with the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.33%), trailing it by over 180 percentage points.

Recent findings suggest that taiwan Semiconductor dominates the foundry market and maintains a strong net margin despite operating in a capital-intensive business. It also pays a modest dividend.

Sources indicate that I think there are too many unknowns tied to Intel's strategic transformation. Taiwan Semiconductor looks like a better buy for 2027 and beyond.

Data Residency Was The Easy Part

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ​A manufacturer can keep every sensitive file within the required geographic boundaries and still lose control over where its information goes.
  • It has been revealed that enterprise data sovereignty, or an organization’s control over how its data is used and which laws govern it, has traditionally been approached through data residency policies and regional infrastructure.
  • According to recent reports, when an AI workload processes enterprise information, that data may pass through services operating beyond the jurisdiction where the original file resides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nick Burling, Chief Product Officer at Nasuni.

Recent findings suggest that ​A manufacturer can keep every sensitive file within the required geographic boundaries and still lose control over where its information goes. An AI application processing that information through a service operating in another jurisdiction may be enough to introduce sovereignty risks.

It has been revealed that enterprise data sovereignty, or an organization’s control over how its data is used and which laws govern it, has traditionally been approached through data residency policies and regional infrastructure. But those safeguards can only go so far when applications process that information across national borders, potentially subjecting it to different legal requirements.

According to recent reports, when an AI workload processes enterprise information, that data may pass through services operating beyond the jurisdiction where the original file resides. The source data can remain within its required geographic boundaries while information derived from it is processed elsewhere.

If an enterprise wants to scale AI without compromising sovereignty, it must be able to deploy workloads wherever they deliver the most value while maintaining demonstrable control over the information those workloads use.

The difficulty is that even routine AI use cases can introduce jurisdictional exposure. A financial services organization might store customer records in Europe to meet data residency requirements, then use an AI assistant to analyze them. While the original files remain in Europe, the assistant could send information to a model operating in another jurisdiction, raising sovereignty concerns even though the source data remains exactly where it belongs.

These secondary data artifacts deserve greater scrutiny because they can contain sensitive information even when they appear removed from the original documents. They may also persist in logs long after an AI interaction ends, creating additional exposure that organizations need to account for.

It has been revealed that under the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, transfers of personal data outside the European Economic Area are subject to specific conditions and safeguards. Meanwhile, the U.S. CLOUD Act allows authorities, through qualifying legal processes, to require providers subject to U.S. jurisdiction to produce data within their custody or control, regardless of its storage location.

These laws confirm why the location of an AI provider’s infrastructure tells only part of the story. The provider’s legal jurisdiction also determines which authorities may compel access to the information it handles.

Keeping every AI workload within the same jurisdiction as its source data may seem like the safest approach. For a hospital processing sensitive patient information, local execution may be necessary. A manufacturer analyzing internal production data, however, could have greater flexibility in using specialized models from external providers.

It has been revealed that applying identical restrictions across these use cases can unnecessarily limit AI adoption. Organizations should be able to choose where each workload runs based on its regulatory requirements while retaining the flexibility to use specialized AI capabilities where appropriate. That may mean keeping sensitive workloads within private infrastructure and allowing others to use external services under established safeguards.

Hybrid architectures provide that flexibility, provided governance extends across the environments involved. This becomes especially important as organizations move from AI assistants toward autonomous agents.

It has been revealed that autonomous AI agents make these decisions more complex. Unlike applications that respond to individual user requests, agents can independently access information and interact with services across different environments. Each interaction can introduce another jurisdiction into the workflow, making it harder for organizations to maintain consistent control over sensitive data.

Sources indicate that the practical priority is ensuring that sovereignty policies follow information throughout an AI workflow. That starts with understanding the information an application can access and the restrictions attached to it. A document containing regulated personal information may require different processing controls from an internal knowledge article. Those distinctions need to inform which services can access the material and where processing can occur.

Those policies must extend to the information AI generates, which can carry the same sensitivity as the original documents. Organizations need to control how that information is retained and who can access it, with visibility into the providers handling it. Sensitive portions of a workflow can then remain within approved infrastructure while other functions run elsewhere.

Industry observers note that finally, organizations need evidence that these controls are working. An audit trail that records who accessed a source file provides limited visibility into what happened afterward. AI governance increasingly requires tracing subsequent processing steps, including which service handled the information and, where relevant, where outputs were retained.

Recent findings suggest that this level of accountability can also support adoption. When enterprises can demonstrate that an AI workload operates within established boundaries, they have a stronger basis for approving it for production use.

Industry observers note that A organization may have complete records of where its sensitive files are stored and still struggle to explain what happened to that information once AI accessed it. Without that visibility, sovereignty becomes difficult to enforce and even harder to prove.

You can’t prove sovereignty for what you can’t trace. Organizations that can provide that evidence will have greater freedom to adopt AI without compromising control.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s going to be easier to rack up extra benefits if you’re a frequent Hyatt customer in 2027.

  • The additions to the Milestone Rewards are designed to give members more choice and personalization, according to Laurie Blair, senior vice president of global marketing and loyalty at Hyatt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s going to be easier to rack up extra benefits if you’re a frequent Hyatt customer in 2027. World of Hyatt revealed upcoming Milestone Rewards, the ability to stack awards (such as Free Night Certificates and Suite Upgrade Awards) on a single stay and a simpler 365-day expiration on all awards.

Sources indicate that the news expands on the fresh details revealed Nov. 17, 2026, around World of Hyatt’s partnership with Delta SkyMiles, which was first announced in September.

The additions to the Milestone Rewards are designed to give members more choice and personalization, according to Laurie Blair, senior vice president of global marketing and loyalty at Hyatt.

"We’re shaping the future of World of Hyatt around what our members value most. After a year of listening, one thing is clear: members want more distinctive benefits, more freedom to use their awards and the opportunity to choose awards that matter most to them,” Blair said in an email to NerdWallet.

But top-tier Globalist members will soon have to choose between perks that they previously received automatically. Most notably, Globalists will no longer receive free parking on award nights in 2027. Instead, they can choose a Free Parking Award as a Milestone Reward that they can apply to award or paid stays.

The Delta Air Lines and Hyatt partnership will also mainly benefit frequent flyers and hotel guests. With the exception of the limited-time intro promotion, only Delta or Hyatt members with elite status will earn points in both programs. Hyatt elites will have to purchase premium tickets on Delta — not economy — to earn Hyatt points on the flight.

Here’s a breakdown of what’s changing:.

Starting Jan. 1, 2027, World of Hyatt will extend Milestone Rewards to guests who have not yet qualified for the first level of elite status. Southwest Airlines did the same in its recent revamp to give loyal customers a thank you before they’ve reached any level of elite status.

World of Hyatt members will reach the first Milestone Reward at just 10 nights or 20,000 Base Points. Previously, it was 20 nights or 35,000 Base Points.

The reward choices at the first milestone are:.

A tier-qualifying night credit, which gets you closer to the next level of elite status.

A $25 FIND Experience credit (Hyatt’s platform for local experiences such as cooking classes).

A $30 spa credit good at Hyatt Inclusive Collection resorts.

According to recent reports, the latter two will likely still require you to pay money out of pocket to use them, as the credit will only cover a portion of your bill. For example, the cheapest spa treatment at Secrets Playa Mujeres Golf & Spa Resort in Cancun, Mexico, will still run you $109 (or $79 after the credit).

The Milestone Rewards start to get good at the higher tiers. Starting at 20 nights, you can select from the existing Milestone Rewards, as well as newly introduced items. Some of the new options include:.

A Delta Air Lines eCertificate.

Free parking on award nights is going away as a Globalist tier benefit. In 2027, a Free Parking Award will be an option that Globalists can select at the 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights The parking award can be used on either a qualifying award or paid stay for up to seven nights.

Hyatt remarked in a call with NerdWallet that roughly 70% of Globalists weren’t using the free parking benefit at all.

Globalists who have earned status in 2026 for 2027 will be grandfathered into the automatic free parking on award stays through their tier expiration date in February 2028.

Sources indicate that to use these latest awards, the Hyatt booking process is also getting an upgrade. Previously, awards like Suite Upgrade Awards and Free Night Awards couldn’t be redeemed on the same stay. Starting in 2027, members can combine eligible awards on a single reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and Free Parking Awards.

The newly introduced booking system will also make it easier to pay for some nights of a single reservation with awards, points, cash or a combination of points and cash.

Industry observers note that every award earned going forward will also carry a 365-day expiration from the date it’s issued, replacing the patchwork of different validity windows. Previously, Suite Upgrade and Guest of Honor Awards expired at “rest of year plus 14 days,” which was just a tad confusing. Meanwhile, Free Night Awards earned through Milestone Rewards were valid for 180 days from the date of issuance, which was not a lot of time to blueprint a trip.

The Milestone Rewards kick in next year, but the other big change around the Delta partnership is available now.

Hyatt elite members can earn World of Hyatt Bonus Points on eligible Delta flights (Delta Comfort, Premium Select, First Class and Delta One). Basic Economy or standard Main Cabin fares will earn nothing from this partnership at all.

Discoverist members earn 1 Bonus Point per $2 spent.

Explorist, Globalist and Lifetime Globalist members earn 1 Bonus Point per $1 spent.

Delta Medallion members (Silver through Diamond) can earn 1 Delta mile per $1 spent at participating Hyatt properties, on top of their regular Hyatt points.

Even if you don’t have elite status with either program, it’s still worth linking accounts to take advantage of the upcoming bonus point promotions:.

It has been revealed that those who link their accounts and complete a qualifying Hyatt stay from Nov. 17 to Dec. 31, 2026, will earn one bonus Tier-Qualifying Night Credit.

Sources indicate that A second bonus point offer runs Jan. 4 through Feb. 15, 2027, for members who take their first Delta flight or Hyatt stay after linking their accounts. Members will earn 1,000 Delta SkyMiles after the Hyatt stay or 1,000 Hyatt points after their first flight in a premium cabin on Delta.

Hyatt and Delta are also holding a sweepstakes through Nov. 23 — no points or miles required to enter — for a free three-night trip for two at Alila Mayakoba in Riviera Maya, Mexico, plus two $1,000 Delta gift cards. Linking your accounts before entering gets you a bonus entry.

If you are interested in dual accrual in 2027, there are some routes to elite status through travel credit cards. Hyatt’s entry-level elite tier comes as a benefit of holding the World of Hyatt Credit Card, but Discoverists earn Hyatt points at half the rate of Explorist and Globalist elites on premium Delta fares.

Sources indicate that you want a travel credit card that prioritizes what’s key to you. Here are some of the best travel credit cards of 2026:.

Flexibility, point transfers and a large bonus: Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

No annual fee: Wells Fargo Autograph® Card.

Flat-rate travel rewards: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Bonus travel rewards and high-end perks: Chase Sapphire Reserve®.

Luxury perks: American Express Platinum Card®.

Business travelers: Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card.

#27354. Industry News: ​Before You Launch Anything, Ask For The Truth

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (904 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: ​Before You Launch Anything, Ask For The Truth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nine PE-backed CEO and COO seats; 50+ acquisitions.
  • When I was a kid, my grandfather gave me one piece of advice about books: read autobiographies.
  • That advice has stayed with me through 30 years of running technology companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russ Reeder is CEO of KeyDelta. Nine PE-backed CEO and COO seats; 50+ acquisitions. We fix the operating model before AI goes in.

When I was a kid, my grandfather gave me one piece of advice about books: read autobiographies. If they tell the truth, you’ll learn something.

That advice has stayed with me through 30 years of running technology companies. A story, a strategy or a product plan is only useful if it’s honest about what doesn’t work. And the person least able to see what doesn’t work is usually the one who built it.

I’m living that right now. This month I finished the manuscript for a book on leadership. Before it goes into production, I’m sending it to a small group of trusted readers: close friends, mentors and leaders I respect. After this many drafts, I know what I meant. I need to know what a reader gets.

The same step belongs before every launch a leader makes: a upcoming strategy, a product, a reorganization or an AI pilot. Many leaders skip it. Or worse, they ask for approval and think they asked for the truth.

According to recent reports, when a CEO presents a proposal, the room tends to nod. That isn’t always agreement. Often it’s the safest thing to do in front of the person who controls budgets and careers.

Sources indicate that nokia shows how expensive that can get. INSEAD’s Quy Huy and Aalto University’s Timo Vuori interviewed 76 managers, engineers and outside experts and found that fear shaped how information moved inside the company. Some middle managers stayed silent or passed up filtered, optimistic information, while top managers pushed for faster delivery on an incomplete picture. Everyone shared the ambition. The facts got softer at every level.

A head nod is not a commitment. If the only feedback you’ve collected came from people who report to you in a meeting you ran, you’ve collected approval.​.

It has been revealed that I learned this the hard way. At a managed services organization I led, our AI engineers built a system that automatically filled in support tickets. Months later, the support reps still weren’t using it. In a weekly standup, the engineers asked why.

The head of customer support answered: “I don’t know why they’re not using it. I haven’t asked them.”.

Recent findings suggest that the call went silent. We built the tool around how managers described the work, not how reps did it or how the work should be done. Once we asked, we had to start almost from scratch. We rebuilt the second version around the outcome the customer needed, and it could resolve certain issues without anyone touching the ticket.

Industry observers note that the truth was available the whole time, but nobody went to get it. Your trusted readers should include the people who will use, deliver or be measured on what you’re launching. Their view is the one a leadership meeting rarely hears.​.

“What do you think?” invites politeness. Specific questions invite the truth. Here are the three I’m asking my readers. I believe they also work for almost any launch:.

1. Where did you stop believing it? This may be where a claim felt too clean, a number too convenient or a timeline too optimistic.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Where did you see your own work in it? That tells you which parts are landing and which are abstract.

Industry observers note that 3. Where did you lose interest? Every strategy has a section people skim. Find it before your customers or your board do.​.

It has been revealed that ​Then go first. Tell them what you’re worried about. In my experience, people are far more willing to point out a problem after the leader has named one.

Feedback that changes nothing teaches people to stop giving it. Before you ask, settle three things:.

It has been revealed that 1. Who owns the changes. This should be one name, rather than “the team.”.

It has been revealed that 2. When the review closes. Aim for a specific date so the feedback leads to a decision instead of an open-ended debate.

It has been revealed that 3. What would change the plan. Write down what you would need to hear to delay, redesign or stop. If nothing could change it, then don’t ask. You’re not asking for feedback. You’re asking for applause.

Sources indicate that when you get answers you don’t like, thank the person who gave them. The first honest critic sets the price for the next one. If candor costs them something, it will be the last honest answer you get.​.

This step comes before production for a reason. A sentence is easy to change in a manuscript and expensive to change in print. A process is easy to fix on a whiteboard and expensive to fix after it’s built into software. A strategy is easy to adjust before you’ve funded it and expensive to unwind once teams are executing it.

Sources indicate that the truth costs the least before you launch. After that, your customers will tell you anyway, and they won’t be as kind. Find the people who will tell you where they stopped believing you, and ask them while you can still use what they say.​​​.

History makes it very clear that the dividend can be volatile, as highlighted by a dividend cut during the 2020 bear market. But there's more to this story than that one dividend cut. Here's what you need to know.

In a recent development, AGNC Investment is a REIT, a special corporate structure designed to pass income on to shareholders. As long as a REIT distributes at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders, it avoids corporate-level taxation. Shareholders have to treat REIT dividends like regular income. (If you hold a REIT in a Roth IRA, however, you can avoid paying taxes on the dividends.) Basically, AGNC will likely always pay a substantive dividend because its corporate structure is designed to do just that.

Recent findings suggest that that said, AGNC isn't a property-owning REIT, which is a fairly easy-to-understand business model. It is a mortgage REIT, which means it buys mortgages that have been pooled into bond-like securities. The company's value is essentially the value of its mortgage security portfolio. It earns the difference between its cost of capital and the interest its portfolio generates. There are two crucial facts here.

In a recent development, first, the value of its mortgage securities will change as interest rates rise and fall. The relationship is inverse: rising rates lead to a decline in value, and vice versa. This is crucial right now because rates are rising and AGNC's portfolio value is declining. Meanwhile, rising rates increase the manufacturer's cost of capital and can squeeze its profits. That said, falling interest rates aren't great either. While costs decline and the value of existing mortgage securities rises in that situation, new mortgage securities come with lower yields. There are a lot of moving parts, which makes AGNC and other mREITs most appropriate for more active investors.

This discussion hasn't even looked at what can happen during a bear market. Dislocations like that can cause unexpected outcomes. For example, during the 2020 bear market that accompanied the coronavirus pandemic, interest rates fell, the value of AGNC's portfolio declined, and it cut its dividend.

According to recent reports, at the time, AGNC tied the cut directly to the decline in the value of its mortgage security portfolio. It also noted that the cut would allow it to invest for the future. However, the dividend has remained static since that cut. Meanwhile, the cash the mREIT generated in the third quarter of 2026 to pay its dividend was $0.37 per share compared to a dividend of $0.36 per share. That's not a lot of wiggle room. And it is facing the impact of rising rates on its portfolio, with its value falling nearly 17% in the quarter. To make matters worse, Wall Street is broadly concerned about the risk of another bear market. It isn't unreasonable to be worried about a possible dividend cut.

Sources indicate that as the chart above highlights, however, the dividend has a much longer history of volatility. Note, too, that the stock price has tended to follow the dividend higher and lower. Given AGNC's corporate structure, you are likely to continue collecting dividends through both good and bad markets. But its history makes it pretty clear that the dividend simply can't be counted on if you hope to use it to pay your living expenses in retirement.

Conservative dividend investors generally look for companies that pay consistent dividends, with a preference for dividends that grow steadily over time. That's just not what AGNC has to offer. That doesn't mean it is a bad investment. It simply isn't a good fit for most income-focused investors given its history of dividend volatility. In fact, AGNC Investment makes the most sense if you reinvest dividends and focus on total return. Indeed, for many investors, this mREIT is a diversification tool rather than an income tool.

Corning provides the physical glass and fiber optic cables that move data, while Vertiv supplies the power and cooling systems that keep servers running. Both companies benefit from the same high-level trends, yet their financial profiles and risk factors vary significantly. This comparison evaluates their current performance and valuation to help you determine which fits your investment strategy.

Industry observers note that corning operates in the materials science space, but it is often classified alongside industrial stocks because of its manufacturing breadth. The company serves a concentrated customer base, with Apple Inc. (AAPL -0.25%) being a primary partner for durable cover glass used in mobile devices. Its optical communications segment is currently seeing high demand as telecommunications carriers and hyperscale data center operators upgrade their networks for artificial intelligence. Because a small number of customers account for a high percentage of sales, this customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $17.7 billion, representing revenue growth of approximately 18.8%. Net income for this period was around $2.1 billion, a significant increase compared to the prior year. This growth is largely supported by the company's ability to innovate in optical physics, providing specialized fiber solutions that allow data centers to pack more connections into smaller spaces.

In a recent development, as of its December 2025 balance sheet, its current ratio stands at approximately 1.6x. The current ratio measures a manufacturer's ability to pay short-term debts with its current assets, with a figure above 1.0 generally suggesting healthy liquidity. The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is nearly 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $1.4 billion, providing capital for research and development.

Vertiv focuses on critical digital infrastructure, specifically power management and thermal cooling solutions. Its major customers include hyperscale and cloud providers such as Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -2.27%) and Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +0.05%), as well as enterprise clients like Walmart Inc. (WMT -0.69%). As artificial intelligence chips generate more heat, the demand for Vertiv's liquid cooling systems has accelerated. The tech giant also maintains strategic partnerships to ensure its own supply of semiconductors for power management units.

Industry observers note that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached around $13.1 billion, showing robust revenue growth of about 35.3%. Net income during this time was approximately $2.1 billion, reflecting a net margin of roughly 16%. This significant growth in sales and profitability highlights the intense demand for physical infrastructure as new data centers are built globally to support cloud computing.

According to recent reports, as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.8x. Vertiv's current ratio is nearly 1.5x, indicating a solid buffer between its liquid assets and short-term liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $1.9 billion. This strong cash generation allows the company to reinvest in manufacturing capacity to keep up with its growing order backlog.

Corning faces risks related to its high customer concentration, as losing a major electronics or telecom partner could significantly impact sales. Because much of its manufacturing occurs in the Asia Pacific region, it is exposed to geopolitical tensions and potential trade restrictions. Vertiv is susceptible to shifts in data center spending, as any slowdown in cloud investment by large-scale providers could lead to decreased demand. Vertiv also carries significant indebtedness, and its credit agreements contain restrictive covenants that could limit its operating flexibility. Managing operational costs and supply chain logistics remains critical, particularly when passing on inflationary costs to large, powerful customers.

Vertiv at the moment trades at a lower multiple of future earnings estimates, while Corning appears more attractive when viewed in terms of market value relative to total sales.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Sources indicate that recently struck deals with Meta Platforms (META -0.32%), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA -0.44%), and Amazon's AWS division have led Corning management to believe it can execute on its so-called Springboard program to jump annual sales to $20 billion this year, $30 billion in 2028, and $40 billion in 2030. Each of the deals is in Corning's core area of expertise: fiber optics and connectivity. These are for AI data centers and newly introduced manufacturing plants being planned in the U.S. Much of the new capacity Corning needs to fulfill these deals will come from its own U.S. expansion, reducing its tariff and general geopolitical risk. In its fiscal 2026 third quarter, sales grew 19%, and net income rose about 60% to $660 million. Wall Street consensus sees net income rising 53% to $2.44 billion.

In a recent development, one of the keys to Corning's growth is sharing its development intends with major customers well in advance, allowing it and its partners to tweak plans and development as needed to better meet future needs. The addition of upcoming AI customers also helps reduce its risk of overreliance on Apple, which makes the iPhone glass, among other products.

It has been revealed that so which is the better buy for 2027? Corning's continual improvement of its fiber-optic and connectivity products has led to impressive growth, with much more on the way. Vertiv, too, is executing well on its position, meeting an essential data center construction need. Still, while Corning comes at a premium, its plans to more than double sales by decade's end seem to offer great promise for long-term investors.

#27348. The Urgency Premium: The Clock AI Can't Control

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (923 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

The Urgency Premium: The Clock AI Can't Control

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adam Thier is the Chief Product and Technology Officer at Anaplan, a leading AI-driven scenario planning and analysis platform.
  • In a recent development, one of the most hyped benefits of AI is that it will speed up decision making from weeks to minutes.
  • Sources indicate that but as any technology leader who’s tried to operationalize AI knows, moving fast means nothing if the rest of the world doesn’t move as fast as you do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adam Thier is the Chief Product and Technology Officer at Anaplan, a leading AI-driven scenario planning and analysis platform.

In a recent development, one of the most hyped benefits of AI is that it will speed up decision making from weeks to minutes. It’s a good story, and parts of it are already true.

Sources indicate that but as any technology leader who’s tried to operationalize AI knows, moving fast means nothing if the rest of the world doesn’t move as fast as you do. ​.

It has been revealed that here’s a simple example that has nothing to do with AI and everything to do with why “faster decisions” alone won’t fix the problem. ​.

It has been revealed that you have a document that needs to arrive at your client’s office on Friday. If you send it a week ahead of time, it costs $0.82, the price of a first-class stamp. Wait until two days before, and it costs maybe $12. The day before? The cost of express delivery can jump to over $30. ​.

In every version, the mail truck didn’t get faster because you decided faster—all that changed was how much of its schedule you had left to use. ​.

Recent findings suggest that most leaders write this off as a rounding error, a one-time tax on poor planning. But the same dynamic plays out across hiring, procurement, sales and product launches. In each, waiting can destroy significant value.​​.

Industry observers note that I call this the “urgency premium,” the avoidable value lost to insufficient lead time. ​.

Industry observers note that there’s a tendency for leaders to treat lateness as binary: you either hit your deadline, or you didn’t. But value deteriorates long before the deadline arrives, whether or not anyone notices. ​.

Technology is especially exposed to the urgency premium because some of its most critical resources disappear quickly. I’ve seen this play out repeatedly leading product and technology organizations.

Recent findings suggest that for example, consider a product launch that’s scheduled for three months out. At this stage, you have multiple implementation partners available, time to secure specialized engineering support and plenty of runway for technical reviews and testing.

If you wait until one month out, you may still be “on track,” but the conditions for reaching your launch look very different. Here’s how: ​.

1. Your options disappear. There is no alert when the specialist you wanted commits to another project, a competitor moves first or a technical decision becomes too costly to revisit. Options disappear while the project still looks healthy on a dashboard.

Industry observers note that ​2. The remaining options get more expensive. Once the preferred path is gone, preserving the same delivery date comes at a premium. Contractors replace internal expertise; vendors charge for expedited support; and overtime fills gaps that more lead time would have avoided. On a $1 million procurement commitment, even a modest rush premium can translate into thousands of dollars in avoidable costs before you even count the preferred suppliers you no longer have access to.

Industry observers note that 3. The quality of execution declines. Technical reviews get compressed, vendor evaluations become less thorough and teams make trade-offs they wouldn’t have made with adequate lead time. You pay more and get less. ​.

It has been revealed that the specialist who commits to another project, the vendor whose calendar fills up, the review that takes however long it takes—all run on clocks you don’t control. Repeat those issues across dozens of projects at enterprise scale, and an organization can stay consistently “on time” while quietly leaving millions on the table. ​.

AI can help you decide in seconds instead of weeks, but it can’t move any of those clocks. ​.

Most organizations plan backward from the last possible date an action can be taken.

My take: That’s the wrong target. By that point, your highest-value options are likely already gone. Instead, leaders should track option cliffs, or the points where a preferred resource, path or choice stops being available. ​.

Let’s go back to the product launch example. The launch date is one deadline, but there are many others hiding in the months leading up to it.

There is a date when your preferred implementation partner can no longer guarantee availability, and a point when compressing testing or security review begins to compromise quality. Those are the cliffs leaders need to identify before work begins. ​.

To find them, ask three questions for all major decisions:.

Sources indicate that 1. How fast do costs escalate as time runs out?

Recent findings suggest that 2. How fast does execution quality decline?

In a recent development, 3. When do your best options actually expire? ​.

Of the three questions, the third is especially important. If a preferred option disappears weeks before a launch, managing to the launch date means managing to the wrong deadline. ​.

It has been revealed that not every decision should be made as early as possible. Sometimes waiting has real value. Requirements may become clearer, markets may shift and new information can lead to better decisions.

Make that trade-off explicit: what you gain by waiting has to be worth more than the options you’ll lose, the costs you’ll incur and the execution quality you’ll sacrifice. ​.

AI may make decisions dramatically faster, but that only makes timing more notable.
