By Ben Gran – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:21AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

One of the biggest stories on Wall Street this week is the resignation of Jensen Huang, former CEO of Nvidia (NVDA -0.44%), caused by a shocking scandal involving extramarital affairs and a romantic relationship with a possible Chinese spy. Many investors are worried that Huang's departure could lead to weaker performance for his firm, negative spillover effects for the entire semiconductor industry, or even a broader downturn in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

It's crucial to keep in mind that the stock market is much bigger than one manufacturer and one CEO. And Jensen Huang's departure is just one factor affecting Nvidia's stock price, which was already in significant decline before the scandal broke. As of Nov. 13, Nvidia shares have dropped by about 7% over the past week, by 13.5% in 2026, and by nearly 33% since reaching a record high on Oct. 6. Since Nov. 13, the stock has been turbulent, with a slight bounce in pre-market trading on Nov. 18 following its latest earnings release.

But if you own S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.33%) exchange-traded funds (ETFs), there's no reason to panic about Nvidia's scandal and a possible further sell-off in the stock. Let's look at a few reasons why.

Industry observers note that jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

In a recent development, if you own individual shares of Nvidia, and the stock makes up a significant percentage of your portfolio, you might want to think carefully about whether you're still bullish on the manufacturer's future without Jensen Huang. Even though Huang resigned, the Nvidia scandal might not be over yet. There are significant risks and uncertainties facing Nvidia, regardless of who the CEO is.

Sources indicate that as of this writing, Huang and Nvidia have not been accused of criminal wrongdoing. But Huang and the company are likely to face further investigations. And more news about the scandal keeps coming out. Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a Chinese businesswoman who was also an alleged Chinese spy. And according to reporting from The Information, this alleged spy might have used her relationship with Huang to gain access to billions of dollars' worth of cutting-edge Nvidia semiconductors, which she then helped provide to companies in China.

Industry observers note that but the U.S. government doesn't want Nvidia's best chips going to China, for national security reasons. Nvidia's chips have been subject to targeted export controls since 2022. Again, this is hypothetical -- no one has accused Jensen Huang or other Nvidia employees of violating export controls or other U.S. laws. The company has remarked that it has no reason to believe that Nvidia corporate secrets or U.S. national security were compromised and has denied any knowledge of Nvidia chips being smuggled into China.

But what happens if more bad news comes out, or an investigation finds that the company violated export control laws or SEC regulations? What if the U.S. tightens its export controls on advanced semiconductors, making it harder for Nvidia to sell its chips worldwide? That could be more bad news for Nvidia stock going forward.

It has been revealed that this is a lot of complexity and uncertainty, and it might be more than Nvidia shareholders want to accept. Even after a solid earnings report, the stock could have further to fall.

Nvidia is one of the largest stocks in the S&P 500. As of Sept. 30, it was the largest holding in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.27%), making up about 8.4% of the fund's assets. As of Nov. 12, after its recent sell-off, Nvidia has fallen to second place in the S&P 500 index, making up about 6.15% of the index.

What if Nvidia stock falls further from here? Let's say the stock goes into another 10% decline by the end of 2026. That's bad news for individual shareholders. But if you own Nvidia through an S&P 500 ETF, that one stock makes up only about 6.15% of the fund's portfolio. If that one stock drops by 10%, the fund's value would only drop by about 0.62%.

Recent findings suggest that in this example, even if Nvidia declines by another 20% from its Nov. 12 share price, an S&P 500 ETF's Nvidia holdings would only decline by about 1.24%. And that doesn't mean the ETF would automatically go down along with Nvidia. Nvidia is only one stock; the other 499 companies in the S&P 500 index might go up. Just because one stock goes down doesn't mean all the stocks or sectors will follow.

Industry observers note that other semiconductor stocks or AI stocks might go up even if Nvidia goes down. Investors might shift money into other companies that they believe will be more competitive in the future if Nvidia struggles to recover. The S&P 500 is constantly sorting and rebalancing itself as some companies gain or lose market cap.

The S&P 500 is not guaranteed to go up or be a "safe" investment. The entire stock market can still go down by 10%, 20%, or more in any given year. But the S&P 500 tends to be steadier than any individual stock, and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has delivered annualized returns of about 12% over the past five years.

NYSEMKT · As of 9:31 AM ET 11/18/26.

The Nvidia scandal shows the value of diversification. It's easy to be confident about individual stocks when the economy is booming, and everything is going well. But when crisis hits, prominent CEOs resign in disgrace, and companies are suddenly thrust into uncertainty and face allegations of serious misconduct, that's when putting too many eggs in one stock's basket can hurt investors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rajat Bhargava is an entrepreneur, investor, author and currently CEO and cofounder of JumpCloud.
  • Industry observers note that the technology industry is racing toward bigger AI breakthroughs, from autonomous agents to increasingly sophisticated models.
  • Recent findings suggest that getting there requires more than adding another tool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rajat Bhargava is an entrepreneur, investor, author and currently CEO and cofounder of JumpCloud.

Industry observers note that the technology industry is racing toward bigger AI breakthroughs, from autonomous agents to increasingly sophisticated models. Inside most organizations, however, the most valuable opportunities are less exciting. They sit in repetitive tasks such as preparing customer handoffs, reviewing sales opportunities, compiling reports and managing routine IT requests. These activities rarely make headlines, but they consume time employees could spend solving problems or building customer relationships. For business leaders, the question isn’t how much AI an organization can deploy but how much better it operates because of AI.

Recent findings suggest that getting there requires more than adding another tool. Organizations need to understand where employees lose time, improve the processes behind that work and define what success looks like. They also need to recognize that AI agents acting on employees’ behalf create upcoming responsibilities around access and oversight. Moving quickly matters, but deploying AI everywhere is not a strategy. The organizations that gain the most will start with everyday problems, test their assumptions and expand what works.

A common mistake is starting with technology rather than a business problem. Leaders may pursue ambitious AI projects while overlooking smaller workflows that could deliver value sooner. Consider a sales representative preparing for a customer meeting by gathering account details, reviewing past conversations and summarizing open issues across several systems. AI could handle much of that preparation, leaving more time to understand customer needs. The goal isn’t necessarily to replace a process; it’s to remove the administrative work slowing it down.

In a recent development, A useful starting point is to ask employees which repetitive tasks consume the most time without requiring much judgment. Rather than launch a company-wide initiative, leaders can evaluate promising workflows against three practical criteria:.

• Find Recurring Bottlenecks: Prioritize tasks that happen frequently and slow down employees or customers.

• Set A Baseline: Record how long each task takes, how often errors occur and what delays cost.

• Test Before Expanding: Pilot one defined workflow, then compare speed, accuracy and employee feedback with the original process.

In a recent development, even a promising workflow may not be ready for automation. When teams follow different procedures or store information in disconnected systems, AI can reproduce confusion at greater speed. Automating customer handoffs, for example, won’t help if sales and customer success disagree on which details must be shared. Before deployment, organizations should clarify responsibilities, standardize the process and agree on a successful outcome. Fixing these gaps first prevents teams from spending money automating inefficiency.

AI makes it easier to produce content, process information and complete routine tasks, but more output doesn’t automatically mean better performance. Thousands of AI-generated sales summaries won’t matter if they don’t improve customer conversations. Weekly reports add little value if nobody uses them to make decisions. Counting prompts, agents or completed tasks therefore offers an incomplete picture of progress. What matters is whether AI improves the quality, speed or cost of a meaningful business outcome.

Each initiative needs a baseline and a result that can be checked after deployment. Customer support leaders might measure resolution time alongside customer satisfaction, while IT teams could track how quickly routine requests are handled without weakening security. Sales teams could examine whether automated preparation creates more time for conversations that move opportunities forward. Measurements should include the effort spent checking AI output and correcting mistakes. If automation saves 30 minutes but requires 20 minutes of rework, the real gain is only 10 minutes.

It is essential to distinguish time saved from value created. Giving employees five hours back each week sounds promising, but the benefit depends on what happens next. That time might support faster customer service, more thoughtful decisions or stronger relationships, none of which is captured by an automation dashboard alone. Small pilots help teams test those connections before committing to larger investments. Scaling then becomes a decision grounded in results, not excitement about the technology.

Sources indicate that an assistant summarizing a document presents different risks from an agent updating customer records or acting inside business systems. As AI moves from answering questions to taking action, organizations need clearer rules about who and what can access sensitive information. A recent report our tech giant conducted found that 72% of surveyed organizations reported a moderate-to-large gap between what AI was permitted to access and what they could prove it accessed. That gap highlights why productivity and oversight cannot be treated as separate projects. Agents need clear ownership, limited permissions and records of their activity from the start.

In a recent development, before deploying an agent, IT and security teams should define its task, permitted systems, approval requirements and accountable owner. An agent preparing a sales report might need to read CRM data but not modify customer records or open unrelated financial files. Access should be restricted to what’s necessary and removed when the task or agent is no longer active. Activity logs should help teams investigate mistakes and identify unusual behavior. These safeguards make it easier to expand automation without losing visibility or control.

Recent findings suggest that governance cannot end when a pilot goes live. Business needs change, employees encounter exceptions and automated workflows can drift away from their original purpose. Teams should regularly review accuracy, outcomes, permissions and whether an agent is still needed. Frontline employees should remain involved because they often spot problems before a dashboard does. The real advantage in enterprise AI will come from improving ordinary work, measuring what changes and keeping control as automation grows.​.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

It has been revealed that nvidia (NVDA -0.44%) had plenty to prove when it reported its fiscal third-quarter earnings after the market closed Nov. 17. It was the tech giant's first earnings report since Jensen Huang's sudden departure. Investors wanted to know whether the artificial intelligence chipmaker could maintain its momentum without its longtime CEO.

The numbers were outstanding. But I think the most important figure in Nvidia's earnings report wasn't its revenue, earnings, or even its guidance for the current quarter.

That's how much Nvidia now expects its revenue to grow in fiscal 2028, up from its previous forecast of 70%. And that increase tells us something key about the company's confidence in its ability to keep delivering AI processors to customers – even without Huang running the show.

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (ending Oct. 25, 2026), Nvidia reported revenue of $115.84 billion, up 103% from a year ago, and topping analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion. Its data center business generated $107.6 billion in revenue, up 110% year over year, as demand for AI computing infrastructure continued to grow.

Industry observers note that "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said. "Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.".

Nvidia also projected fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $130 billion, ahead of the $125.1 billion consensus estimate compiled by LSEG. While that number stands out, it's also notable to know that Nvidia's fiscal fourth quarter includes an additional week of revenue. Melius Research estimates that accounts for approximately $9 billion to $10 billion of the roughly $14 billion sequential increase in Nvidia's guidance.

That's why I'm paying more attention to what Nvidia expects to happen next year.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/17/26.

In a recent development, the increase in Nvidia's fiscal 2028 growth forecast is what really got my attention. In August, Nvidia projected 70% revenue growth for its 2028 fiscal year, and acknowledged that its ability to supply enough processors would limit how quickly it could expand.

Now the company is bumping that projection up to 75% growth.

During the organization's earnings call with analysts, Kress said that Nvidia evaluated both customer demand and the additional supply it expects to make available. The company believes it can deliver that growth despite ongoing supply constraints and new U.S. export restrictions.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress. Image source: Nvidia.

Nvidia's ability to grow depends on more than designing powerful chips. It needs manufacturing capacity, advanced memory, packaging, networking components, and customers with enough data center capacity to put its systems to work.

It has been revealed that and just as importantly, Nvidia needs to keep those relationships going even in the post-Huang era. Huang was forced to resign Nov. 12 after the board began investigating allegations that he had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Other extramarital relationships with Nvidia employees also came to light.

Industry observers note that there are some, including President Donald Trump and people at Nvidia, who suggest that Huang be reinstated. And Huang issued a lengthy statement on the social media platform X saying he would return if asked.

But Nvidia closed that door on Tuesday, stating that Huang would not be reinstated and citing his "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.".

Huang's departure created legitimate questions about Nvidia's leadership and its relationships with customers and suppliers. Those concerns won't disappear after one earnings report. But the tech giant's higher fiscal 2028 forecast suggests its manufacturing partnerships, customer relationships, and product roadmap remain intact.

I think the increased forecast is more significant than a quarterly earnings beat. While its first earnings report without Huang suggests the business can continue delivering exceptional results, a revenue growth rate of 75% in the next fiscal year indicates Nvidia is hardly running out of momentum.

#27340. AI Observability 2.0: Why Enterprises Need To Measure The Full Cost And Value Of AI

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (863 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

AI Observability 2.0: Why Enterprises Need To Measure The Full Cost And Value Of AI

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yuri Gubin is Chief Technology Officer at DataArt, working with organizations integrating AI into complex engineering environments.
  • ​As we’re approaching the end of 2026, it’s interesting to look at what we expected from AI this year and what really happened.
  • In a recent development, what we’re still missing, despite all the efforts, is an industry-proven methodology that has become a standard for AI-enabled development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yuri Gubin is Chief Technology Officer at DataArt, working with organizations integrating AI into complex engineering environments.

​As we’re approaching the end of 2026, it’s interesting to look at what we expected from AI this year and what really happened. If you go back a few years, many of the predictions were based on guesstimates and wishful thinking. Now we do see that AI is everywhere, agentic development is quite good and there are methods evolving with examples of how AI really boosts development. We also see the impact on individual productivity, even outside engineering, in knowledge management and other areas.

In a recent development, what we’re still missing, despite all the efforts, is an industry-proven methodology that has become a standard for AI-enabled development. We have different frameworks explaining the stages of AI adoption, and examples of what works and what doesn’t, but we’re still some way from having an approach that everybody can use, regardless of which LLM they’re working with.

And then there’s the ROI question. We still need better measurements and evidence of the benefits, particularly when it comes to understanding whether the same approach will work in different environments. This is where observability could become particularly interesting.

Organizations will be rethinking the costs of AI, and I’m not talking about subscriptions or tokens alone. It’s the cost of data, infrastructure and everything you put in place to make AI happen in your manufacturer. All these expenses add up, and we’ll likely see more scrutiny and greater demands for results.

This is already happening, of course. We’ve been anticipating this and advocating for reasonable use of AI, where you validate results with data rather than relying on expectations. Some organizations will try to spend less without substantial changes in quality or delivery, and others will spend more, but this rethinking is already underway.

If you look at the work companies were doing three or five years ago, they were paying for people, cloud infrastructure and other operational expenses. Now you may be doing the same work, but you’re also consuming AI resources, and the value of that work may be different. So the economics change, including margins and how companies capture the value created. This may affect business models across the board, including outside IT services.

Industry observers note that one area we’ll likely see developing is observability, but in a different sense from how we’ve traditionally understood it. Before, we would talk about operational telemetry and system metrics, while with AI, we need to understand where it’s being used and how much value it has created.

I would call it AI Observability 2.0, because there should be a new standard and a new wave of technologies that help us understand the impact of AI.

Right now, I don’t think the ecosystem is there to tell us exactly how much we spend on each action when we consider the end-to-end flow. And it’s not only about pure numbers. You have the technology, the decision-making, the judgment, the quality of the result, the spending and the value created. We need to understand the entire chain, including what happens when something doesn’t work well and how we can troubleshoot, evaluate and react faster. Some of this may come through newly introduced technologies, or it may be changes to the same technologies we’ve had in our toolboxes before.

It has been revealed that one thing we still haven’t resolved is how to measure ROI in a way that gives us reliable, repeatable results. Let’s say AI works well in one team and you see productivity improvements. If you apply it to another team, even within the same organization, will it work the same? The technology stack might be different, the problem space is different and it’s difficult to say whether you should expect the same benefits.

There’s something similar happening with data. Its importance was already on everyone’s mind at the beginning of 2026, but as you start making progress, you discover new depth to the challenges you already knew about.

You may have created a data lake and put all the data in one place, but then you discover that it doesn’t help you improve the use of AI as much as you expected. Maybe the conventional data lake is too slow, or maybe you’re still missing some data. You wanted to transform the company, and now you realize that having the data in one place doesn’t necessarily solve the problem.

Recent findings suggest that I hope 2027 will be a year of AI growth, but in a more reasonable, pragmatic and mature way, rather than explosive experimentation. Hopefully, as an industry, we’ll make progress on methodologies and standards for AI-enabled development, because those are still to be defined.

It has been revealed that I also expect technologies that help us understand the value AI creates will become more important. Observability is an interesting area because we’re still missing that understanding of the complete process, and we’ll need it to make better decisions about AI investments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:38AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Applied Materials ›.

As the race for dominance in artificial intelligence intensifies, choosing the right infrastructure provider is critical. Should you invest in equipment giant Applied Materials (AMAT +0.79%) or connectivity specialist Marvell Technology (MRVL +2.33%)?

Applied Materials supplies the tools that actually build the chips, making it a foundational player in the semiconductor ecosystem. Marvell designs the custom chips and networking components that move data between servers. Comparing these two reveals different ways to play the ongoing shift toward high-performance computing and massive data center expansion.

According to recent reports, applied Materials sells materials engineering solutions used to produce nearly every new chip and advanced display in the world. It serves a concentrated customer base of logic, foundry, and memory manufacturers, including giants like Intel (INTC +1.18%) and Micron Technology (MU -0.92%). Two specific customers accounted for approximately 19% and 15% of net revenue, respectively. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

Industry observers note that in the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached nearly $34.4 billion. This represented growth of roughly 21.4% compared to the prior period, driven by strong demand for advanced chipmaking equipment. Net income totaled approximately $10.1 billion, showcasing the profitability possible at this scale.

It has been revealed that as of Applied Materials' October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3. This ratio measures total debt against shareholder equity, with lower numbers typically suggesting less financial leverage. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is roughly 2.3. For those following semiconductor stocks, strong cash flow is vital for R&D. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $6.2 billion.

Marvell Technology operates as a fabless supplier, meaning it designs high-end semiconductor solutions but outsources the actual manufacturing. The company focuses on data center core networks and the network edge, serving original equipment manufacturers and cloud service providers. For its most recent annual reporting period, two customers each accounted for 10% or more of net revenue, and the 10 largest customers collectively accounted for 82% of net revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $9.5 billion. This figure reflects growth of close to 30.6% over the previous 12 months as the company expanded its footprint in AI infrastructure. Net income for the same period was approximately $2.6 billion, marking a significant turnaround from previous years.

In a recent development, as of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.3. Its current ratio is approximately 2, indicating a solid ability to meet short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was close to $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Applied Materials faces significant geographic concentration, with a heavy reliance on customers in China. This exposure makes the company sensitive to trade policies and export restrictions. It also manages legal risks involving export controls, including a $252 million settlement reached in February 2026 for export violations involving Semiconductor Manufacturing International. Furthermore, its reliance on complex global supply chains creates vulnerability to regional disruptions or inventory obsolescence.

It has been revealed that marvell Technology has high customer concentration. Its 10 largest clients account for nearly 82% of revenue, and it often competes with rivals like Broadcom(AVGO +2.46%). The manufacturer is also navigating a massive $115 billion pending acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE +2.56%). This deal introduces risks related to shareholder dilution and the complex process of integrating two large organizations. Additionally, Marvell's dependency on third-party foundries in the Pacific Rim creates supply chain risks if regional political conflicts arise.

Applied Materials right now appears to be the more conservative value choice, while Marvell Technology commands a higher premium given its faster growth profile.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Sources indicate that the forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, helping you see how much you are paying for every dollar of projected profit. The P/S ratio measures the market price relative to sales over the past 12 months.

Industry observers note that marvell and Applied Materials are riding the current tech boom, with both stocks hitting all-time highs earlier this year. They've since pulled back a considerable amount, but they're still handily outpacing the S&P 500 (^GSPC -1.03%) by massive margins:.

In a recent development, there's not a ton of daylight between the two stocks' recent returns. And as for business performance, Applied Materials has a slightly higher net margin, while Marvell is posting stronger revenue growth.

According to recent reports, I lean toward Applied Materials in this matchup. Marvell's revenue growth is impressive, but its pending acquisition of Lumentum introduces a fair amount of risk. There's the possibility of dilution, but there's also the potential that the combined organization doesn't create the cost-savings and synergies management had hoped for. That could lead to significant writedowns, which would almost certainly impact the stock negatively.

Applied Materials just seems to have less risk, which makes it my pick for 2027 and beyond.

#27336. Does Intelligence Need The Railroad?

Does Intelligence Need The Railroad?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charles Yeomans is the chairman and founder of Atombeam.
  • Industry observers note that ​In Fortune’s recent Term Sheet (paywall), Allie Garfinkle asked investor Hans Tung to take the Industrial Revolution analogy for AI seriously, which he did.
  • Recent findings suggest that as history, I find the argument persuasive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Yeomans is the chairman and founder of Atombeam.

Industry observers note that ​In Fortune’s recent Term Sheet (paywall), Allie Garfinkle asked investor Hans Tung to take the Industrial Revolution analogy for AI seriously, which he did. His argument runs from Britain’s steel steamships to the railroads that helped decide the American Civil War, and he casts data centers as the railroads of this century. The models that make a difference, he argues, are the ones with the infrastructure behind them: “The models that win are the ones that are available.”.

Recent findings suggest that as history, I find the argument persuasive. As a prediction, it rests on an assumption almost nobody examines: that intelligence has mass. We have accepted it as settled that AI needs all of this infrastructure. We should be asking whether that is a fact about intelligence or a fact about one design.

Sources indicate that railroads were important because cargo was heavy. Steel ships became critical because trade goods had to cross oceans in hulls. Data centers matter today because the dominant AI architecture makes every act of machine intelligence heavy. A large language model answers a question by driving it through billions of calculations on specialized processors, and it does so again for the next question, and the next, forever. Usage rises, and the compute bill rises with it. Under that architecture, Tung is simply right. Intelligence must ship to the railhead, and the nation with more track wins. One estimate he cites puts the American buildout at an average of 3.6% of GDP every year into the next decade, which tells you how heavy we have decided intelligence has to be.

But heaviness is a property of the architecture of AI. The way our brains work suggests there is a different way to build machine intelligence: Hold knowledge as durable structure, and compute each answer directly from it. The engineered version can go one step further than biology: The structure can be explicit and inspectable, so a machine can show the basis for what it concludes. In a system built this way, learning is the expensive step, and it happens once. After a subject is learned, producing an answer would be computationally trivial, small enough to run on an ordinary processor, with no round trip to anyone’s railhead.

According to recent reports, we do not need much compute to identify a car when we see it, or a person we know. Our brains run on 20 watts, not megawatts, so we know this kind of efficiency is possible. The economics would be the reverse of the token meter: Cost falls as the machine learns, because knowledge would persist instead of being recomputed. Something else follows from structure: A machine that computes from what it actually knows can decline to answer when it does not, instead of generating a plausible guess. The reliability problems keeping AI out of high-consequence work are, at root, the same architecture question.

In a recent development, if this idea for a new kind of AI proves possible, and prototype work by my own team and others gives me reason to believe it is, the strategic picture inverts in two ways. The first concerns Tung’s own Civil War detail. He points out that most battles clustered near the railroad because the railroad was the dependency, and dependencies are what adversaries target. A force, a hospital or a factory whose machine judgment lives locally needs no railhead; everything stays behind the firewall, and the whole thing runs on the power budget of a laptop, or even less, rather than a substation. Local AI is not just more secure and more available; it steps almost entirely out of the energy problem, because computing an answer from learned structure draws watts where generating one from scratch draws megawatts.

In a recent development, the second is the geopolitical race itself. We need to face the fact that we are betting on out-pouring concrete against China, perhaps the most formidable builder of physical infrastructure on earth. The asymmetric answer to that is not more gigawatts. It is more intelligence per watt, which is an architecture question before it is an energy question.

The railroads will be built, and much of that buildout will be valuable; training, research and the broad models that benefit from scale will use every mile of track. But the assumption that all intelligence must ride those rails deserves the scrutiny we give any assumption worth trillions. Tung claims the winning models are the available ones. I agree. The most available intelligence is the kind that never has to travel.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The artificial intelligence sector of the stock market isn't the most popular place to invest right now.
  • While AI investment sentiment is presently negative, I think there are plenty of great investment opportunities right now.
  • CEO Jensen Huang resigned due to relationships with staff and a potential Chinese spy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Keithen Drury – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:44AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

The artificial intelligence sector of the stock market isn't the most popular place to invest right now. There are questions surrounding how the AI build-out will be allowed to proceed, with Democrats sweeping the U.S. midterm elections. This could put a pause on some data centers, affecting companies that provide the components. Still, many projects are underway, and many builds will likely be allowed to continue as-is, with newer facilities coming under greater scrutiny.

While AI investment sentiment is presently negative, I think there are plenty of great investment opportunities right now. They include Nvidia (NVDA -0.44%), Broadcom (AVGO +2.46%), and Micron (MU +1.10%). While Nvidia is in a bit of a mess with its CEO resigning last week, I think the stock has cratered to the point where it makes sense to buy shares. The other two are also genius buys and make for timely investments, with the market not being bullish on the AI outlook.

First, let's look at Nvidia. CEO Jensen Huang resigned due to relationships with staff and a potential Chinese spy. This is a huge loss for Nvidia because Huang co-founded the tech giant and built it into what it is today. At the same time, Nvidia's products are so impressive and have such a dominant market share that they practically sell themselves. This means business will likely go on as usual at Nvidia, and investors should use the global sell-off as a buying opportunity for the stock.

After the sell-off, Nvidia trades at a dirt cheap price of 10.5 times next year's earnings estimates.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

That's a huge discount, and considering the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.33%) trades for about 20 times forward earnings, I can see Nvidia having an impressive rebound in 2027.

While Nvidia is a timely buy, it still has some troubles. So, investors should also look to other stocks.

Sources indicate that broadcom has been taking market share from Nvidia for a while. Instead of making a broad-purpose GPU like Nvidia, it's partnering directly with AI hyperscalers to develop custom AI chips that are tailored to their workloads. This has major cost advantages, as running workloads on these chips is far cheaper than on GPUs. However, they cannot be used in every situation, so there will always be a large place for Nvidia GPUs.

Next year, Broadcom expects its AI semiconductor revenue to double, and double again in 2028. That's huge growth and will also outperform Nvidia over that time frame. As a result, I think it's a top option to buy in addition to or instead of Nvidia.

Industry observers note that micron is a key supplier to both Broadcom and Nvidia, as it makes memory chips for computing devices. The memory chip industry has seen practically all of its production capacity consumed by the AI build-out, causing chip prices to soar. This has led to a record-setting year for Micron, but it could get even better.

During Micron's latest earnings report, its management team noted that market conditions will be worse in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026. When Micron claims "worse," it means worse for its clients, not for itself. The manufacturer will do well because high demand for memory chips has driven up prices, translating into pure profit for Micron.

Historically, Micron has been a cyclical stock, which is why the market isn't valuing it at its full potential.

MU PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

The market is valuing Micron's stock as if its business will evaporate tomorrow; we know that won't happen for several more years, given the strength of the AI build-out. This mismatch is your investment opportunity, and I think Micron is a top stock to buy now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the manufacturer paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

It has been revealed that mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Recent findings suggest that initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in latest wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

According to recent reports, mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

According to recent reports, enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the organization, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

It has been revealed that while the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In a recent development, in total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto mentioned.

Sources indicate that scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

Dodge ranks No. 476 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.5%. See Brookfield Infrastructure Partners KPIs on TipRanks.

Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 as Xabi Alonso’s team succumbed to their second pre-season defeat.

Mudryk replaced Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute against Juventus, marking his return to competitive football after a long doping ban that was resolved this week thanks to changes in Wada regulations.

There were a couple of crosses delivered from the left flank by the Ukrainian winger, who could yet leave Chelsea on loan or on a permanent basis before the close of the transfer window.

Juventus were the victors though, thanks to a sumptuous 68th-minute goal by Kosovo winger Edon Zhegrova.

Alonso had 21 players on his bench, and made 12 second-half substitutions.

Levi Colwill and Cole Palmer featured in the defeat by 10-man Spurs on Saturday, but sat this game out as they continue to build fitness. Danny Welbeck did start though, reunited with former Brighton team-mate Joao Pedro up top.

Chelsea scored just one goal against Spurs and Juventus, but the thrust provided by right-back Marco Palestra in tandem with first Geovany Quenda and then Estevao was a bright spot for Alonso.

Chelsea continue their pre-season against AC Milan on Saturday, before they host Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge on August 15.

They begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham in the Monday night slot on the opening weekend.

According to recent reports, even Chelsea’s in-house streaming had given up the ghost by the end. Consecutive pre-season defeats for Chelsea, but worth remembering that Colwill and Palmer sat out this fitness exercise and Enzo Fernandez is still to return. Palestra’s performances a real positive but the team is still finding its way.

Juventus win a corner late on, but Yildiz’s delivery is too close to Penders. Just two minutes for Chelsea to find an equaliser.

Mudryk does well to dig out a cross from the left but the goalkeeper Perin gathers. There will be four minutes of added time to play.

Recent findings suggest that chelsea not really threatening an equaliser as the game meanders towards a conclusion. Should they score a goal, we will have a penalty shoot-out.

Estevao looked for Mudryk with a reverse pass between full-back and centre-back but there was too much weight on the ball.

Estevao’s free-kick is saved but the bigger news for Chelsea fans is that Mykhailo Mudryk has been introduced from the bench, replacing Nicolas Jackson for the closing stages.

Lavia and Liam Delap involved in some handbags with the Juventus players, Bremer the centre-back in the thick of things too and has been shown a yellow card. Chelsea have a free-kick, Estevao over it from 35 yards out.

According to recent reports, just the one goal scored for Chelsea against top level opponents in pre-season, but I doubt Alonso will be panicking just yet. Chelsea play Milan this weekend before hosting Real Sociedad on August 15th in their final pre season friendly.

Juventus goalkeeper Perin sells Nicolas Jackson a dummy so he can pick a pass into midfield. The Italian side controlling the game quite well since the goal, against a weaker Chelsea team.

Chelsea’s younger players will have to dig them out of trouble in the last 20 minutes. There has not been much in the game, Chelsea have shaded it in general play without quite creating enough.

In a recent development, the Kosovan winger with a first-time, left-footed hit from almost 25 yards, curled into the top corner. Nothing Penders could do about it.

Recent findings suggest that more changes from Chelsea: Anselmino, Acheampong, Satpaev, Assugo and Delap the players on, replacing Hato, Palestra, Gittens, Caicedo and Pedro. Alonso finishing the team with his younger players on the pitch.

Jonathan David slides a pass across the Chelsea six-yard box when there was a chance to shoot, but the flag was up for offside in any case.

Industry observers note that penders does well to palm away an inswinging cross from Zhegrova, before Estevao picks out the run of Palestra on the break with a brilliant forward pass. Chelsea corner, cleared. Now Caicedo has been booked for a cynical challenge to stop a break, much like Douglas Luiz.

Nicolas Jackson hacked down by Douglas Luiz after he turned on halfway with three or four Chelsea runners in support. Painful one for Jackson, and a yellow card for the former Aston Villa midfielder. Chelsea players not happy with that challenge in a pre-season game.

Chelsea certainly have the upper hand in the game, quick feet from Joao Pedro to win a free-kick in midfield. If either team is going to score the game’s first goal, you fancy it will be them.

This time Chelsea find Palestra with a ball over the top, but his shot at goal is at a comfortable height for the goalkeeper.

Sources indicate that palestra popping up in a centre-forward position again, but his shot towards goal is not struck cleanly. The right-back at the heart of Chelsea’s attacking again.

Two very different XIs out there for the second half.

Penders replaces Sanchez in goal, Sarr on for Tosin, Estevao on for Quenda and Jackson on for Welbeck.

For Juventus: Bremer, Perin, Zhegrova, Owusu and David are on.

In a recent development, not much to write/phone/WhatsApp home about, so far. The combination between Quenda and Palestra down Chelsea’s right has been the best feature of their football, am sure we will see Estevao on that flank in the second half among other changes. The bumpy pitch and a hydration break has not helped the spectacle.

There will be four minutes of stoppage time, simply a result of the hydration break.

Far too much space opens up between Chelsea’s defence and midfield, with Meritti turning and carrying the ball forward. Boga tests Sanchez with a strike from the edge of the box. That was probably Juventus’s most threatening attack.

Palestra defends well as the last man up against Milik, Chelsea almost undone by Locatelli’s outside of the foot pass.

Robert Sanchez caught under a cross swung to the back post, very unconvincing goalkeeping, but Juventus could not get their shot away in the box. Nicoll-Jazuli then did well to bring the ball away for Chelsea at the edge of the box.

According to recent reports, chelsea have another corner, and yet again it comes from a right-sided attack. Chelsea are in ascendancy now after a slow start, but it is a very low intensity contest.

It has been revealed that caicedo with a couple of threatening crosses from a centre-right position, but no Chelsea player can connect with them cleanly. Gittens’s dribbling down the left causing problems for Cambiaso, and he was the one attacking Caicedo’s cross at the back post.

Sources indicate that play has now resumed after the drinks break. No changes from either team, those will come at half time. Chelsea have 21 players sitting on their bench, albeit a number of academy players are on tour.

Time for a hydration break, even though the game is being played under a closed roof.

Recent findings suggest that chelsea’s right side is their most dangerous, by a distance. Quenda does well to slip Palestra in on the overlap, and his low cross into the six-yard box is cleared for a corner. Juventus clear. Boga with a burst through the Chelsea midfield but the Juventus man then gets his pass wrong.

Kelly with a left-to-right switch to Cambiaso, and his cross deflects off the toe of Miretti in the middle and trickles just wide of the far post. Sanchez was scrambling but I think the goalkeeper had it covered.

Chelsea enjoying their most sustained spell of possession in Juventus’s half so far, without quite carving out a clear cut chance. Juventus defending their penalty area with a back five, but they do not have Bonucci, Chiellini and Barzagli back there anymore.

Quenda with a threatening inswinging cross from the right flank, but Welbeck could not quite rise high enough to direct his header towards the far corner. Quenda was keeping the width for Chelsea with Palestra inside the winger in the box. Quenda then slices a shot over from long range.

Welbeck and Caicedo involved in some good combination play, with Nicoll-Jazuli’s outside of the foot pass finding Gittens. Chelsea’s left-winger runs into traffic, but he has been one of the bright spots of the pre-season campaign thus far.

Will be interesting to see if they can find a way for him and Reece James to start games. Chelsea as a team yet to find much rhythm in the game so far.

Tosin could well find himself down the pecking order this season among Chelsea’s raft of centre-backs, but he makes an important block in the area before Locatelli drags a shot wide from the edge of the box.

Former Bournemouth defender Lloyd Kelly is in the Juventus team. The Italian team are looking to press high in the early minutes whenever Chelsea try to play out from the back. Quenda with an early dart at the Juventus defence but he gets the pass all wrong with Palestra overlapping.

Palestra with a loose first touch but he recovers and defends well. Like in Sydney, this looks another very bumpy pitch, you can see the join marks between the pieces of turf that have been freshly laid. Coming out of these games without any injuries will be a priority for Alonso.

#27327. Your AI's Confidence Score Won't Catch Products You Don't Carry

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1024 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

Your AI's Confidence Score Won't Catch Products You Don't Carry

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Srijith Ravikumar is a Principal Engineer at Amazon building AI search and recommendation systems.
  • In 2024, a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to compensate a customer who had relied on its website chatbot’s advice about bereavement fares, and it rejected the airline’s argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions.
  • Ask a recommendation model how confident it is, set a threshold and drop everything below it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Srijith Ravikumar is a Principal Engineer at Amazon building AI search and recommendation systems. Published at ACM CIKM and IP&M.

In 2024, a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to compensate a customer who had relied on its website chatbot’s advice about bereavement fares, and it rejected the airline’s argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions. Retailers face a version of that exposure: AI recommendations for products the store doesn’t carry. A tempting way to decide when to trust those suggestions is a score the model reports about itself.

Ask a recommendation model how confident it is, set a threshold and drop everything below it. That guardrail is easy to build and easy to report upward. In my tests, it barely worked. Across 48 test settings, filtering on stated confidence cut the share of out-of-catalog suggestions by a median of 0.02 percentage points, and in 18 of them, the filtered list came out slightly worse.

It has been revealed that my study measured how often suggestions miss the catalog, not what a miss costs. The likely costs are easy to name. A customer taps a suggestion, finds nothing to buy and trusts the feature a little less. A slot that could have sold something goes to an item that can’t. An assistant that names products the store lacks invites complaints. Treat those as hypotheses to check against your own numbers.

In a recent development, this year I tested four widely used large language models from four different developers. Each suggested 10 items from a user’s history, working from memory with no access to the catalog, on three public datasets covering movies, local businesses and retail toys. I checked every suggestion against the catalog it was meant to come from, using a matching method validated against about 200 human judgments, and counted anything not in that catalog as a miss, whether or not it exists elsewhere.

It has been revealed that the out-of-catalog rate depended heavily on the catalog. Across the four models and three catalogs, it ran from 0.6% to 61%. Every model stayed under 3% on movies and reached roughly half or more on toys, with identical instructions. A rate measured in one domain tells you little about another, and a vendor demo is one domain.

Recent findings suggest that confidence barely moved. Each model’s stated confidence on toys stayed within about four points of its confidence on movies, while its out-of-catalog rate rose twentyfold or more. Researchers have already shown that models stating their own confidence tend to be overconfident, a bias you could at least correct for. Here the bias wasn’t stable. Across the 12 model-and-catalog combinations, the models were underconfident in seven and overconfident in five: All four were underconfident on movies, and all four were overconfident on toys. A correction tuned on one catalog would point the wrong way on the next.

Industry observers note that one explanation fits the data, though the data don’t prove it. Asked how confident it is, a model seems to rate how good it thinks the suggestion is. It can’t check whether the item sits in your catalog from memory.

The filter I used is split conformal abstention, which uses conformal prediction, a standard statistical technique, to drop the least-confident suggestions while guaranteeing that a set share of the good ones survive. Its best result across the 48 settings was a cut of under two percentage points. The method largely kept the good items, as designed. Its guarantee states nothing about removing bad ones.

In a recent development, I tested only the confidence a model states in words. Token probabilities, agreement across repeated samples and constrained generation are different signals I didn’t test, and they may do better. If your model only picks among candidates retrieved from your catalog, the failure changes shape: The risk becomes a poor pick among real items, and this study doesn’t speak to that.

Within that scope, these are the questions I’d bring to a product review, an AI governance meeting or a decision to fund the next phase.

Sources indicate that is every suggestion checked against the live catalog before a customer sees it? It removes items you can’t sell, though it won’t fix relevance.

How was the out-of-catalog number measured? If items are matched by title, the matching rule can move the answer more than the model does. On identical model outputs, plausible off-the-shelf matching rules disagreed on the toy catalog’s out-of-catalog rate by more than a factor of 10. Ask for a check against a couple of hundred hand-labeled cases, with the remaining error reported next to the number. Having the model return product IDs avoids the problem.

Is a promising fix being tested as an experiment? On the business catalog only, I told two models to recommend from a fixed catalog that I didn’t show them and asked how sure they were that each title was in it. Out-of-catalog suggestions fell from 12.9% to 1.5% for one model and from 14.4% to 8.9% for the other. Each cut is at least three times the filter’s best result. The paper reports the figures and compares the first cut directly against that result. That prompt changed the instruction and the confidence question at once, and it covers two models in one catalog. Before a rollout, ask for a test that changes one prompt element at a time, runs on a held-out sample of the live catalog and reports both the out-of-catalog rate and whether the suggestions stayed relevant.

In a recent development, was it measured on your own catalog, including the long tail of products customers rarely look for? A benchmark from someone else’s data, or a pilot on your bestsellers, claims little about those.

Keep the confidence score for sorting results or deciding where a person looks first. The governance question is a different one: What share of our AI suggestions aren’t in our live catalog, measured across the long tail? The confidence score can’t answer it.​.

By Jake Lerch – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:45AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Airbnb ›.

Industry observers note that will the future of growth be driven by global travel experiences or the expansion of independent digital commerce? Deciding between Airbnb (ABNB -2.82%)and Shopify (SHOP -4.00%)involves choosing between two very different platform leaders.

According to recent reports, airbnb connects millions of travelers with unique stays, while Shopify provides the software backbone for modern retail. Both companies benefit from powerful network effects, where more customers or merchants make the platform more valuable for everyone involved.

Industry observers note that airbnb operates as a massive marketplace for lodging and experiences, connecting more than 5 million hosts with guests in roughly 220 countries. In its latest annual report, the manufacturer highlights its reliance on Amazon (AMZN +0.05%) for platform hosting and its use of third-party providers for community support. As the platform evolves, it is exploring the use of AI in travel to enhance its search capabilities and host support.

Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $13.9 billion. This represents a revenue growth of approximately 16.7% compared to the prior twelve-month period. During the same time frame, the firm reported net income of nearly $3.2 billion.

It has been revealed that as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures a firm's ability to cover its short-term debts with liquid assets, reached roughly 1.4x. The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is approximately 0.3x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $4.6 billion, though note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.

Recent findings suggest that shopify serves as the central operating system for millions of merchants across 175 countries, providing tools for both online and in-store sales. The organization supports everyone from small entrepreneurs to large enterprise brands, relying on partners like PayPal and Stripe for payment processing. This ecosystem approach allows it to scale without owning inventory, creating a software-centric business model with high recurring potential.

Industry observers note that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached close to $14.2 billion. This reflects a revenue growth of roughly 32.5% over the preceding period. Shopify also reported a net income of approximately $2.1 billion for these twelve months.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 6.0x, indicating a strong ability to meet short-term obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.0x, indicating a very low level of debt relative to equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $2.0 billion, and stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.

Industry observers note that airbnb faces significant regulatory hurdles, such as the restrictions on short-term rentals in Fresh York City, which could be adopted by other global cities. The firm also competes intensely with major travel platforms like Booking Holdings (BKNG -1.95%), Expedia Group (EXPE -0.07%), and Trip.com Group (TCOM -1.00%), as well as search engines like Alphabet. Furthermore, an ongoing IRS tax audit involving a $1.3 billion claim adds a layer of financial uncertainty to the company's long-term outlook.

It has been revealed that shopify encounters fierce competition from established e-commerce software vendors and massive marketplaces like Amazon. The business is also exposed to cybersecurity risks and data privacy concerns, which have previously led to class action litigation over its collection of buyer information. Since Shopify relies heavily on third-party payment service providers, any disruption in those relationships could impact its ability to process transactions for its merchants.

Recent findings suggest that airbnb appears to be the more conservatively valued stock, carrying both a lower Forward P/E and a lower P/S ratio compared to Shopify. The Forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio is the market cap divided by sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

In a recent development, when comparing Airbnb and Shopify, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.

Firstly, we should consider revenue growth. Here, Shopify can claim an advantage. Over the last three years, the company has averaged year-over-year revenue growth of 28.7%. What's more, in recent quarters, that growth has accelerated, with Shopify delivering 31.6% revenue growth in its most recent quarter. Airbnb's three-year average is 13.5%; its growth has also accelerated, with the company reporting 17.7% revenue growth in its most recent quarter.

It has been revealed that another factor to consider is each tech giant's profitability. Both companies have been consistently profitable in recent years. However, Airbnb can claim an edge in the category. Its operating margin is 22.6%, while Shopify's is 18.1%.

Finally, there's valuation. Since both companies are delivering consistent profits, let's use price-to-earnings (P/E) to compare their valuations. Airbnb stock trades at a P/E multiple of 34x, while Shopify trades at around 87x. That makes Airbnb stock significantly more affordable.

Recent findings suggest that to sum up, investors may want to consider both of these consumer stocks, given their impressive growth rates and profits. However, in this particular head-to-head comparison, Airbnb has the overall edge, in my view. The manufacturer's profitability, combined with its more reasonable valuation, complements its revenue growth, which exceeds 15%, making it my choice in this battle of consumer stocks.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:50AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Docusign ›.

Deciding between established software leaders and high-growth infrastructure providers involves weighing profitability against potential. Investors today are comparing Docusign (DOCU +0.48%) and Fastly (FSLY +0.25%) to see which fits better in a long-term portfolio.

Docusign dominates the digital agreement space, while Fastly powers the speed and security of the modern internet. While both operate within the software-as-a-service model, they serve very different niches. This comparison examines their financial health, growth trajectories, and valuation to help you determine which stock aligns with your investment strategy for 2027.

Recent findings suggest that docusign is a prominent name among tech stocks, providing an intelligent agreement management platform. The company has moved beyond basic e-signatures to help organizations automate the entire lifecycle of a contract. With over 1.8 million customers, its software integrates deeply with major enterprise systems from Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM -1.79%), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -2.27%), SAP (SAP -4.84%), Alphabet Inc. (GOOG -1.30%), ServiceNow (NOW -0.17%), and Workday (WDAY -0.58%).

In a recent development, in the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached about $3.4 billion, representing growth of approximately 8.6%. The company also reported a healthy net income of roughly $329.9 million during this period. This steady expansion highlights how Docusign is managing to maintain growth even as its core electronic signature market becomes more saturated.

Sources indicate that as of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, is nearly 0.1x. Its current ratio of approximately 0.7x suggests that short-term liabilities presently exceed its cash and other liquid assets. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was close to $1.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 53.4% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because it is a non-cash expense added back.

Industry observers note that fastly provides an edge cloud platform designed to help developers build, deliver, and secure digital experiences at high speeds. The organization serves global enterprises, particularly in the media and entertainment sectors, including major accounts like TikTok. Partnerships with Comcast Corp. (CMCSA -1.13%) and Jio Platforms further extend its reach. However, its top 10 customers generated roughly 32% of revenue in the 12 months ended December 2025, suggesting a degree of customer concentration.

Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached around $719.1 million, which is growth of roughly 21.5% over the previous period. Despite this double-digit top-line expansion, the tech giant reported a net loss of approximately $62.9 million. This loss reflects the ongoing costs of scaling its global infrastructure and investing in its edge computing capabilities to compete with larger rivals.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintains a current ratio of approximately 2.6x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term obligations with current assets. Its debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.5x, showing a moderate level of debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $65.8 million. However, note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 124.2% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

Industry observers note that docusign faces substantial revenue dependence on its eSignature product, making it vulnerable if demand for that specific tool slows down. It also deals with intense competition from Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE -4.25%) and emerging generative artificial intelligence providers that could disrupt traditional agreement workflows. Additionally, scaling its new agreement management platform involves significant execution risk, while its global operations must navigate complex international regulatory and data privacy challenges.

Sources indicate that fastly carries risks related to its high customer concentration, particularly its reliance on major accounts like TikTok for a significant portion of its sales. The company competes against established content delivery networks like Akamai Technologies Inc. (AKAM +0.95%) and Cloudflare Inc. (NET +1.84%), as well as hyperscale providers such as Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +0.05%), Google, and Microsoft. Furthermore, any major operational outages could damage its reputation, and the company remains dependent on a limited number of hardware suppliers.

Docusign is cheaper by Forward P/E, tracking future earnings estimates, while Fastly leads on P/S ratio measuring sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

For Docusign, sales in its current fiscal year are seen growing by nearly 9% to $3.5 billion, with a slightly better percentage gain in net income to $346 million.

In a recent development, docusign's launch and global expansion of the IAM platform with the introduction of AI-powered tools should position the manufacturer for future growth. However, the not-so-great projected revenue growth rates suggest that Docusign may be entering a phase of more mature growth and a landscape of increasingly competitive digital agreement and contract management software. In particular, news reports OpenAI would launch a ChatGPT product that would compete head-on with Docusign in the document summary field caused some investor fears. Right now, however, the signature and identity verification part of Docusign's business appears unthreatened by ChatGPT.

Recent findings suggest that fastly, meanwhile, processes over 5 trillion requests a day, a huge number that is actually just a small part of the total addressable market (TAM) for the business. Management sees the TAM as $22 billion, giving it a long runway for growth. The company has posted three straight quarters of more than 20% growth (year-over-year).

One of the company's competitive edges, it says, is that it delivers its resources dynamically, allocating them in real time to whatever the load is on a global basis. So, for example, one Thursday night, its network might be delivering Thursday Night Football. On Black Friday, the exact same network is handling e-commerce. The next week, it might be handling a video game release. Fastly says that makes it a much more efficient network than competitors, who have siloed networks for security, compute, and delivery, et cetera.

For the current fiscal year, look for sales to grow to $741 million, a 19% rise over the prior year, with a much narrower net loss of about $72 million.

It has been revealed that fastly shares come at a premium to Docusign's, at least through the prism of forward P/E, but it brings along faster growth for the price. For 2027, Fastly is the stock that's the better buy here.

Tech Report: Your AI Roadmap Is Really A Planning Problem

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Monisha Somji | Senior Digital Transformation & AI Executive.
  • According to recent reports, walk into almost any large enterprise today, and you will find AI everywhere: copilots in the inbox, pilots in every function, a steering committee or two.
  • In my experience, the pattern is consistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monisha Somji | Senior Digital Transformation & AI Executive.

According to recent reports, walk into almost any large enterprise today, and you will find AI everywhere: copilots in the inbox, pilots in every function, a steering committee or two. Yet the financial results rarely match the activity.

In my experience, the pattern is consistent. The demo works, the pilot succeeds and the initiative stalls anyway because nobody owns the step between a working prototype and a changed way of working.

The data agrees. McKinsey’s latest global survey found that 88% of organizations now use AI in at least one business function, but only 39% report any enterprise-level EBIT impact, and just 6% qualify as “high performers.” Gartner predicts that “over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls.”.

Sources indicate that the usual explanation is that the technology is not ready or that employees need more training. Having led digital transformation and product programs across technology, retail and mobility, I see a different culprit: the planning and funding machinery wrapped around the model.

Recent findings suggest that across industries, leaders often avoid saying out loud that this is a leadership problem, not a technology problem. Pilots are popular because they are politically safe. They let every executive show AI progress without consolidating a team, giving up a budget or killing a sponsored project. Redesigning a workflow forces decisions about who owns it, who loses control of it and what stops.

Recent findings suggest that those decisions are hard because incentives point the other way. Leaders are rewarded for launching initiatives, not retiring them. Budgets belong to functions, not workflows, so no one gains by consolidating. Risk teams are measured on avoiding incidents, so they review late and cautiously. Everyone behaves rationally inside a system that quietly rewards the wrong thing.

According to recent reports, most large organizations still run on annual budgets, quarterly planning and intake queues designed for software that ships a few times a year. AI capabilities shift in months. A use case approved in one cycle can reach production two cycles later on a model already a generation behind.

Industry observers note that that is why McKinsey’s research keeps landing in the same place. Of the 25 organizational attributes it tested against EBIT impact, workflow redesign had the strongest effect. The companies capturing value are not adding a tool to an old process. They are rebuilding the process.​.

Every function runs its own AI queue, with its own vendors and its own definition of success. It is common to find three teams funding near-identical summarization tools from three vendors, each unaware of the others, until a budget review puts the requests side by side.

Industry observers note that A pilot gets a budget and a deadline. When the money ends, the initiative ends, whether or not it worked. Pilots routinely hit their targets and still die because the funding line closes the same quarter the results arrive and no one owns the workflow they were meant to change.

Risk and privacy reviews arrive after the build, as a gate. A team builds for months, meets risk review for the first time at launch and a two-week review becomes a two-month rework. According to a Gartner analyst,​ many current agentic efforts “are mostly driven by hype and are often misapplied,” which is what happens when use cases are chosen before anyone tests them against value and risk.

Sources indicate that consolidate the front door. Create one intake and prioritization path for AI work, shared by product, technology and the business. One view of demand makes it possible to sequence work, reuse components and kill duplicates early.​.

Sources indicate that the next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by whoever licenses the most capable model, because those models will be available to everyone. It will be won by organizations that decide quickly, fund the right workflows, govern as they build and change how work actually gets done.

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
